items.title: Ontario was warned about career college with skyrocketing OSAP growth, letter shows
items.description: A career college with student financial aid usage that government data shows grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not among those the minister cut off this spring, and a letter newly obtained by The Canadian Press shows he was specifically warned about the school more than a year earlier.

items._ogDesc: A career college with student financial aid usage that government data shows grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not among those the minister cut off this spring, and a letter newly obtained by The Canadian Press shows he was specifically warned about the school more than a year earlier.
items.body:
A career college with student financial aid usage that government data shows grew thousands of per cent in a few years was not among those the minister cut off this spring, and a letter newly obtained by The Canadian Press shows he was specifically warned about the school more than a year earlier.

The college itself strongly denies any wrongdoing.

Career Colleges Ontario flagged in a January 2025 letter to the ministry that the association was concerned about unusually high growth in Ontario Student Assistance Program usage at 10 campuses.

The names of most of the schools were redacted when a copy of the letter was filed in court this year, but an unredacted copy obtained by The Canadian Press shows that the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology topped that list.

“As an association that represents career colleges in Ontario, we are concerned about how schools with increases exceeding 2,000 per cent in submissions, such as CCBST … with a 2,696.26 per cent increase, are accommodating these students effectively while upholding educational standards,” executive director Kate Bartz wrote.

That growth of nearly 2,700 per cent was over two years.

Government data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request shows that in 2021-22 there were 74 students accessing OSAP, and in 2024-25 there were 4,481 students — an increase of nearly 6,000 per cent.

A statement from a lawyer for the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology says it did not experience anywhere near a 6,000 per cent increase at any of its campuses and suggested that number comes from “what is at best an inability or failure to understand the financial information that is contained in government records.”

Allan Dick wrote that the college’s records indicate enrolment increases of less than 1,900 per cent.

“Insinuations that CCBST has been involved in fraudulent wrongdoing are not just categorically and simply denied,” he wrote. “They are false. And the very premise that these insinuations are based on is false.”

Dick said the college has provided auditors KPMG, who Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn has tasked with a system-wide audit, with detailed explanations for its growth. It was well-placed to deliver online programming at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic due to technology advances it had implemented, and one campus was relocated and it attracted many more students, he wrote.

“The college was aware of allegations of improper conduct in the industry and how such conduct was allegedly being undertaken,” Dick wrote.

“The college never participated in these activities. It made all efforts in real time and in response to the available information to ensure its enrolling students were legitimate, attended their classes, did their assignments and fulfilled their placement obligations in order to graduate.”

The school’s other three campuses in the Greater Toronto Area were also on Career Colleges Ontario’s list, but the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was not among six schools the government cut off from OSAP eligibility in May.

Quinn is defending the fact that OSAP kept flowing to the school until last month by saying the data the ministry was receiving was evolving.

“I think ultimately, we’re running multiple investigations at the same time, and that would be one of the ones that we are investigating, and once that threshold is met, that’s when we act, as we have earlier this year,” Quinn said, referring to both removing six schools from eligibility in May and a sector-wide pause on OSAP he enacted early last month.

He said Monday that once data showed “they were worse than what we initially thought, that’s when we put a pause,” referring to when he stopped OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions last month.

Liberal critic Tyler Watt said the minister’s explanations don’t make sense.

“You either didn’t catch it or you knew and chose to do nothing about it, so which one is it?” he said. “If this (school) was the top of the list, wouldn’t that be your No. 1 priority to investigate?”

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said she questions the strength of the ministry’s investigations.

“We have heard no answers from the government as to how this was allowed to happen,” she said. “Any actions that the government took were far too delayed to try to protect the integrity of the OSAP program.”

Dick said there is a simple explanation for why the minister did not lump Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology in with the six schools it cut off from OSAP in May.

“CCBST never had the ministry put the brakes on its programs because it never engaged in any improper conduct,” he wrote. “Any suggestion that the ministry was lax in its assessment of the college through its usual audit processes is simply unfounded.”

Quinn has said that preliminary findings of a KPMG audit into career colleges and OSAP are so troubling that he has referred the matter to the Ontario Provincial Police. He has not named any specific schools associated with that police referral.

The Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology had previously not responded to multiple requests for comment.

In May, the province ended OSAP eligibility at six campuses, the same schools that the federal government had flagged concerns about a year prior. The number of students receiving OSAP increased between about 650 per cent and 1,375 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25 at those schools.

The students at four campuses in total in 2024-25 accounted for about $151 million in provincial grants, according to the data.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

Allison Jones, The Canadian Press

items.body:
TORONTO — A book about Canada’s evolving immigration policy by Globe and Mail columnist Tony Keller has won the $30,000 National Business Book Award.

The organization behind the award announced “Borderline Chaos: How Canada Got Immigration Right, and Then Wrong” as the winner of the prize at a ceremony in Toronto on Thursday.

Published by Sutherland House Books, the book offers an analysis of Canadian immigration polices and how to move them forward.

The annual prize recognizes Canadian authors whose work demonstrates exceptional research, originality and relevance to contemporary business challenges.

The runners-up for the prize included Lawrence Stevenson for “Inside SNC-Lavalin: How Crime and Politics Almost Killed a Great Canadian Company” and Scott McIntyre for “A Precarious Enterprise: Making a Life in Canadian Publishing.”

The winner was selected by a jury that includes members from business and academic sectors.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

Kaitlyn McGrath, The Canadian Press

items.title: Artists are quitting Instagram and Facebook over fears AI will steal their work
items.description: A wave of AI-generated artwork is taking business away from the creators themselves, and is especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[CNN spoke with over a dozen artists on how they are navigating the current AI landscape. (Ekaterina Goncharova / Moment RF / Getty Images via CNN Newsource)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: A wave of AI-generated artwork is taking business away from the creators themselves, and is especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook
items.body:
Matty Burnham, a watercolour artist in the United Kingdom, said he discovered a Pinterest account impersonating his illustration in 2024. The account created AI versions of his watercolours and listed them on fake profiles via Shopify, Facebook and Instagram, he told CNN.

Although Burnham tracked the Pinterest account to Ho Chi Min City, Vietnam, he does not know who was behind it.

It’s part of a wave of AI-generated artwork that’s taking business away from the creators themselves, and is especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook. CNN spoke with over a dozen artists on how they are navigating the current AI landscape.

AI-generated art profiles “monetize Facebook,” Burnham said. “They have hundreds of thousands of followers who believe these fake profiles are genuine artists and direct users to various websites with shops and ads.”

The problem has pushed some independent artists to pull back from Instagram, Facebook and other Meta platforms, especially with the tech giant’s proposed updates to its terms of service. Some have considered leaving Meta-owned social media platforms entirely, pausing posting or turning to other online creator communities such as Patreon or Substack.

Tim O’Brien, board member at the Society of Illustrators, said he believes artists deserve meaningful consent, fair compensation and accessible ways to challenge unauthorized exploitations of their work.

“For many artists, this is not merely a legal dispute. It is a question of livelihood, creative ownership, consent and basic fairness,” O’Brien said.

Meta’s updated terms would still allow automated software to scrape external websites and extract large amounts of data without permission from business account owners. This includes personal portfolios, online stores, and links to Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads business accounts.

The terms were originally supposed to go into effect Oct. 30, then got pushed back to Nov. 20. The company announced on Nov. 5 that the updates were delayed indefinitely.

“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.

Still, even with the latest delay, the proposed updates have already caused another wave of artists to leave Meta.

Samantha Waldron, co-owner of Dutcher Photography in Madison, Wisconsin, told CNN that she deleted all business and personal Facebook pages earlier this month and has since transitioned her Instagram business accounts to personal accounts, deleted a vast majority of posts, and removed all external website links from Meta account bios.

“It was the last straw that was a long time coming. I’m frankly relieved not to have to worry about keeping up on social media moving forward,” said Waldron.

Under the updated terms, independent artists’ images, style, and property could be scraped without their knowledge to train generative AI models, creators told CNN. Those AI models could then replicate or replace human-made art — and potentially impact artists’ businesses on those sites.

Megan Wimberley, founder of Cowgirl Artists of America in Tulsa, Oklahoma, is in the process of deleting all of her Meta accounts. She told CNN that she considers these new terms a major breach of trust. Wimberley believes everyone – not just artists – should be concerned about posting their personal images, video and audio due to potential AI scraping.

“I actually view Meta as a company trying to lead the way in AI and that their social media platforms are no longer really about social media but more about free licensing to train their AI,” said Wimberley. “If you’re a mother and you’re posting your children, you’re potentially licensing Meta to use your children to train their AI.”

Some even chose to “go dark” on Meta platforms from Oct. 30 through Nov. 6 when the updated Meta terms were initially planned to kick in, refraining from posting or sharing content in protest of the updated terms. Wimberley said she started the “Meta blackout” campaign on Oct. 22, and it took off from there.

Nicole McKay, artists relations director at The Guild of Artists and Artisans, told CNN in a statement that many artists in the United States have begun removing their accounts from Meta platforms in response to the upcoming policy change with AI model training. Many artists have posted “goodbye” messages on Instagram and Facebook, citing Meta’s politics.

“For artists who rely on these platforms to showcase and sell their work, connect with customers, and build their businesses, leaving Meta presents a difficult choice between protecting their work and maintaining their livelihoods,” McKay said.

Artists traverse ‘AI slop’

AI-generated artwork has serious repercussions on the creator economy, artists told CNN. Online imitators are forcing artists to change their strategy on how they reach an audience.

Andrew Scott, a contemporary artist in Rochester, N.Y., said he directly messaged an AI art impersonator in September about copying his work.

He said the person admitted to using Scott’s original work as a starting point to build her own AI-generated art videos. The person behind the impersonating profile then shared AI clips on Instagram, giving the impression she created the actual art. Scott noted one of her posts with AI artwork received 50 million views.

Scott said he explained to the impersonator how the AI versions could potentially hurt his business. She has since unfollowed him on social media but continues to create the AI-prompted knockoffs, he said.

Nancy Chen, a ceramic artist in Canada, posts videos on social media that show how she makes sale pieces. But she understands those clips could also be vulnerable to AI model training. Chen says she’s been wary lately of posting polished images of her work on Meta platforms but hasn’t decided to leave yet.

“It makes me wonder how independent artists can present their work to the world when their transparency can be weaponized,” Chen told CNN. “AI can outpace any individual artist, so I definitely feel some pressure to compete in price, even though I feel my labor is already underpriced.”

One of the main concerns for creators is the scale and speed that AI can push content, especially compared to human-made work that can be time-consuming. That concern is compounded by questions of how generative AI is trained on artwork, usually without artists’ say, and how copyright law applies to AI.

Isaiah Steinfeld, an American Institute of Graphic Arts Board Member who builds with AI, said that protecting artists and embracing the technology don’t have to be opposing views. He noted that artists can still register work for copyright, pursue infringement claims and get unauthorized copies taken down.

For instance, Meta said creators can report instances of AI impersonators and submit takedown requests via its Intellectual Property Reporting Center.

“So, provenance has to cut both ways: protect creators from having their work appropriated and protect people using new (AI) tools from having their actual contributions erased,” Steinfeld said.

Google released an online tool, SynthID Detector, this month to the public. The free site allows anyone to upload a file to check if that image, video or audio file was made by AI from Google and partners such as OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao.

In a press release, Google said the platform has watermarked over 180 million images and video and regularly sees over a million verification requests each day.

But this is only the beginning, and independent artists agree these changes do not go far enough. Many still grapple with whether to share content on social platforms at all, but in their line of work, it’s about brand awareness.

“Personally, I don’t trust that there will be enough done to protect artists,” Burnham said. “The UK government seems more concerned about not limiting profitable start-up tech companies than protecting artists. My hope is that the public continues to reject gen-AI in this current model.”

When CNN reached out for comment, a spokesperson for the U.K. Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “The government has engaged extensively with creatives, industry bodies and AI firms and we are taking time to ensure we find the right approach to this issue.”

“We have been clear that we will not proceed with any course of action which does not work for our creative industries and our AI sector,” they added.

items.title: ‘Slam dunk with our own MPs:’ Government House leader confident Liberals will pass Bill C-39
items.description: Bill C-39 – also known as the Building Canada Strong Act – is designed to speed up federal approvals for major projects and revise federal labour laws.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[People walk past the Peace Tower on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Tuesday, Nov. 4, 2025. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sean Kilpatrick]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu"></media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Bill C-39 – also known as the Building Canada Strong Act – is designed to speed up federal approvals for major projects and revise federal labour laws.
items.body:
OTTAWA – Despite some competing views within the Liberal caucus on climate policy, Government House leader Steven MacKinnon says he is confident the federal government’s omnibus Bill C-39 will pass without whipping the vote.

“It is a slam dunk with our own MPs. We ran on a platform called Building Canada Strong, and this is a bill called Building Canada Strong,” MacKinnon said in an interview with CTV Question Period airing Sunday.

“This is a very important bill, and it has the support of the Liberal caucus,” he later added.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Bill C-39 – also known as the Building Canada Strong Act – is designed to speed up federal approvals for major projects and revise federal labour laws. A House of Commons committee struck to examine C-39 wrapped earlier this week with minor changes made after a marathon study.

But the landmark legislation has garnered criticism for weakening environmental safeguards, infringing on Indigenous rights, restricting workers’ right to strike and rushing parliamentary scrutiny.

In an opinion piece published in the Toronto Star this week, B.C.-based Liberal MP Will Greaves wrote that he is “worried” Canada is losing its climate credibility.

“These are issues that I’ve been raising, and others have been raising since the election,” Greaves said while speaking to reporters on Wednesday when asked about his column. “They’re important issues to many of our supporters across the country and very much to the constituents that I represent.”

While Greaves said he wouldn’t leave the Liberal caucus over the federal government’s shifting climate policies, he wouldn’t say if he would support Bill C-39.

“I haven’t had a chance to speak with the House leader about the amended bill yet. So, I look forward to doing that, and we’ll go from there,” Greaves said.

When pressed by host Vassy Kapelos on Greaves’ criticism, MacKinnon said he is “very confident” the bill will receive the support of the Liberal caucus.

Asked specifically if the party will whip the vote, MacKinnon said that wouldn’t be necessary.

“I don’t think we have to whip the vote,” MacKinnon said. “This is a bill that we all, the principles on which we all ran. We all got elected, and we’re very, very proud to be able to hold this bill up as an example of the great things we can get done for our country.”

The federal government has made the bill’s passing a priority in recent weeks.

On Wednesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he was “absolutely not” concerned about the pace at which the bill is going through the House of Commons and described it as “the most consequential economic legislation” the federal government has put forward.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, meanwhile, is the latest opposition leader to say his party will vote against the bill after the Liberals refused to accept major changes.

“Carney wants a top-down authoritarian economy that favours corporate power brokers at the expense of workers,” Poilievre said in Ottawa on Thursday. “We want a bottom-up, open, free-market economy that allows workers to work, builders to build, and investors to invest. That’s what we will continue to fight for.”

Along with the Conservatives, the NDP, the Bloc Québecois and the Green Party have all signalled they will not support the bill. It means the Liberals will need all the party’s MPs to vote in favour of the legislation for it to pass, as they hold a razor thin majority with 173 seats.

You can watch Government House Leader Steven MacKinnon’s full interview on CTV Question Period Sunday at 11 a.m. ET.

items.title: ‘Kraft Dinner’ budget: Mayor’s comments prompt second protest at City Hall
items.description: Protesters gathered in front of City Hall Thursday afternoon to protest comments made by Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.
items.content: <media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Noovo Info</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Protesters gathered in front of City Hall Thursday afternoon to protest comments made by Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.
items.body:
After starting a swirl of memes, mockery and malcontent over Kraft Dinner comments, protesters gathered in front of City Hall Thursday afternoon to protest Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.

A protest began at 1 p.m. following the nearly 10 per cent tax increase announced earlier this week, followed by Martinez Ferrada’s since walked-back statements.

“It’s just like when you’re putting together your personal budget: If you know you’re going to have less money next year, well, you have to make some choices,” she said in a Quartre95 interview.

“Let’s be honest, maybe sometimes we’ll eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can’t afford filet mignon.”

The mayor recorded a social media post the following day saying “it was pretty tactless.”

“What I meant was that when a city makes choices, it’s the same as when you make personal choices,” she said. “In this instance, the city has to choose between paying for new parks or filling potholes, and I’m going to choose filling potholes.”

Protesters came armed with Kraft Dinner, pans, stoves and ingredients, with the apparent intention to make the Canadian household staple a political flashpoint.

Raúl Garate organized the protest, saying the tax hike will affect home owners, but also tenants.

“I’m not against the fact that we need to take care of our of our city because it is in dire need of love,” he said, adding that he was concerned about the burden on working Montrealers.

“You have people, like working-class people, that struggle so much to make their ends meet that will have to also consider this new tax hike.”

Montreal’s budget increased the average municipal tax rate to 9.8 per cent in Montreal. It was the largest increase in 50 years.

Martinez Ferrada said the increase was necessary to deal with the city’s aging infrastructure, including water mains, housing and homelessness.

Protesters fear the nearly 10 per cent tax hikes will be passed on to renters and hurt the most vulnerable in society.

“Life in Montreal has gotten increasingly expensive, and the comments made by our mayor were beyond unacceptable,” one protester said.

Signs depicting the mayor as Marie Antoinette illustrate the sense here that Martinez Ferrada is out of touch.

“It was completely, not just tone deaf, but it shows the disconnect that she has from Montrealers,” said another protester.

So many memes

Hundreds of viral memes about the Kraft Dinner comments have flooded social media. One expert said this type of content has become a powerful form of political discourse.

“Memes add to the conversation and they add to the feeling of momentum around a politician or an issue. And sometimes that is good momentum, and sometimes that is not so good momentum,” said Colleen McCool, a Concordia University political communications student.

There’s even a website that breaks down the city budget line by line costed out in terms of boxes of Kraft Dinner showing this year’s total spending equal to 3.5 billion boxes.

“I just kind of wanted to use this moment as a hook to show this data in an interesting way. To have citizens kind of exploring this data, reasoning about it, asking like, is this how I picture the budget should be spent?” said Niko Draca, creator of kdgate.ca.

Outside City Hall, many feel the administrations’ priorities are wrong.

“To give $45 million more to the police and raise our taxes by 10 per cent. That’s a choice. We didn’t choose that,” said a protester.

Thursday’s protest was the second one to take place this week, as hundreds of demonstrators gathered on Tuesday. Peter Sergakis, owner of hundreds of residential units, bars and restaurants, organized that protest.

items.title: $168M loan guarantee provided for First Nations’ investment in LNG pipeline
items.description: A dozen First Nations are being provided a loan guarantee to support their investment in a pipeline feeding natural gas to the LNG Canada plant.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Piping is seen on the top of a receiving platform of a natural gas pipeline terminus in Kitimat, B.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 28, 2022. items._ogDesc: A dozen First Nations are being provided a loan guarantee to support their investment in a pipeline feeding natural gas to the LNG Canada plant.
items.body:
VANCOUVER — A dozen First Nations in British Columbia are being provided a roughly $168-million loan guarantee to support their investment in a pipeline that feeds natural gas to the LNG Canada plant. 

It’s the fifth transaction the federal Canada Indigenous Loan Guarantee Corp. has closed since the agency was set up in 2024, with the goal of helping make it more affordable for First Nations, Métis and Inuit communities to share in the economic benefits of major projects. 

The 12 nations that make up the CGL First Nations Limited Partnership are investing in the entity that holds TC Energy’s interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which delivers gas from northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada plant and tanker port Kitimat, B.C. 

“This investment represents a historic milestone for our Nations and a new chapter in our relationship with Coastal GasLink,” said Corrina Leween, director of the First Nations partnership, in a news release Thursday. 

“It reflects years of work to advance Indigenous participation in major infrastructure projects and to create a stronger role for our nations in shaping the economic future of our territories.”

  • Latest updates on company news here

The investment is the second planned Indigenous investment deal related to Coastal GasLink. In October, another group representing five First Nations announced it had invested $65.3 million of its own funds in TC’s Coastal GasLink subsidiary. 

For major projects to happen, the support of affected Indigenous communities is crucial, federal Natural Resources Minister Tim Hodgson said in an interview Thursday. 

“As nations become more comfortable with projects, as they become more comfortable with different forms of participation, we’ll see more and more equity ownership,” he said.

“It’s the ultimate form of ownership in a project because it means you have real participation and upside from the project.”

TC chief executive François Poirier said in a news release that the deal reflects the strength of the relationships the company has developed along the pipeline corridor over more than a decade.

“This transaction demonstrates what is possible when Indigenous communities, industry and governments come together with a shared commitment to creating opportunities that deliver benefits over the long term,” he said. 

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

TC has given the green light to a project that would expand the capacity of Coastal GasLink to serve the second phase of LNG Canada. No new pipeline would be built, but the flow of gas would be increased through pumping power and other upgrades. 

For the pipeline expansion, the LNG Canada partners — Shell Canada and four Asian firms — are taking the lead on construction, reducing the exposure to cost overrun and schedule risks for TC and its co-owners in the pipeline. 

The initial construction of Coastal GasLink encountered numerous challenges, from blockades by opponents in Wet’suwet’en traditional territory in northern B.C. to disruptions from the COVID-19 pandemic. By the time it was complete in late 2023, the cost had ballooned to $14.5 billion from $6.6 billion five years earlier.

“Look how far we’ve come. We’ve come from a place where a project like this, there was no shared vision, to a place where the project is performing, it’s generating revenues for the people of British Columbia, for the people of Canada, and now — really importantly — for the First Nations all along its route,” Hodgson said. 

Within B.C. First Nations, sentiment toward Coastal GasLink is divided. 

A majority of Wet’suwet’en elected band councils supported the pipeline, while some traditional hereditary chiefs resisted it.

“We respect every Nation’s right to self-determination, and the reality is this project destroyed our lands without our consent,” Hereditary Chief Na’Moks said in an emailed statement after Thursday’s announcement. 

TC and the Indigenous groups hold a collective 35 per cent interest in Coastal GasLink, with KKR Co. and Alberta Investment Management Corp. owning the rest. 

“TC Energy is further divesting from CGL, a project for which TC Energy’s estimates for the cost of construction doubled, and now the federal government is encouraging Indigenous finances to back it, tying those to the risk and uncertainty of the pipeline and LNG business,” said Gwii Lok’im Gibuu, a member of the Gitxan First Nation and co-executive director of the Skeena Watershed Conservation Coalition. 

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

items.title: Labour group says Bill C-39 changes fail to protect workers' right to strike
items.description: The Canadian Labour Congress says the modest amendments made to the Liberals’ landmark economic legislation fail to protect the right to strike.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Minister of Jobs and Families Patty Hajdu makes her way to a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Justin Tang]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Justin Tang</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Canadian Labour Congress says the modest amendments made to the Liberals’ landmark economic legislation fail to protect the right to strike.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The Canadian Labour Congress says the modest amendments made to the Liberals’ landmark economic legislation fail to protect the right to strike.

The federal government’s proposed Bill C-39 includes sweeping changes to speed up project approvals across the country, along with adjustments to the Canada Labour Code that would affect strikes and lockouts in federally regulated industries.

Since C-39 was tabled in September, union leaders have been hammering the government over changes that would spell out the labour minister’s power to end work stoppages in designated sectors like ports and railways if the national interest is at stake.

A House of Commons committee struck to examine C-39 wrapped earlier this week and made a few adjustments to the Labour Code sections of the legislation.

One set of changes affects a new special mediator role proposed by the legislation. The amendments lay out a process to appoint the mediator and gives that individual powers to dictate the schedule for mediation between the parties.

Another change would require a post-mortem study in Parliament every time the minister uses the powers in the legislation to quash a strike. That would include a debate in the House of Commons over whether the intervention was justified.

Siobhan Vipond, executive vice-president at the Canadian Labour Congress, said in an interview Thursday that Ottawa already has the power to intervene when work stoppages put the national interest at risk -- by tabling and passing back-to-work legislation.

Adding a retroactive analysis after a strike has been quashed does not protect the rights of workers on the picket line, she said.

“Afterthought has its place, but not instead of actually having rights,” Vipond said.

The consequences for bargaining in C-39 revolve around proposed amendments to Section 107 of the Labour Code. The federal government has used that section multiple times in recent years to end strikes affecting Canadian ports and railways and other federally regulated businesses like Canada Post.

Whether existing legislation already gives Ottawa that power is the question at the heart of multiple ongoing court challenges. The government argues C-39 doesn’t grant any additional powers and instead puts “guardrails” on the use of Section 107 by adding the national interest condition and the need to consider the special mediator’s report.

The Canadian Labour Congress proposed amendments that would have established that Section 107 cannot be used to scuttle a legal strike. The group proposed the creation of an independent panel that could recommend back-to-work legislation in the event of an “extraordinary national emergency.”

Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has promised not to compromise the right to strike.

In a media statement sent to The Canadian Press on Thursday, Hajdu’s office said that proposed changes to the Labour Code are the product of hours of consultation with stakeholders over the spring and summer, in addition to more than 100 hours of witness testimony at the C-39 committee.

The Liberals held a majority of seats on that committee, giving them ultimate control over which amendments were adopted.

“Together, these changes will help build a modern, resilient, and fair labour relations system that supports good jobs, stable workplaces, and a stronger Canada,” the statement from Hajdu’s office says.

Derrick Hynes represents Canada’s major railways, ports and airlines and telcos as the CEO of Federally Regulated Employers -- Transportation and Communications, or FETCO.

Hynes said Thursday that C-39 is a “strong step in the right direction” after high-profile work stoppages at rails, ports and airlines in recent years. Proponents of C-39 argue Canada must protect its critical supply chains from disruption, particularly as Ottawa works to secure new export markets and sell the country as a destination for foreign investment.

Hajdu told reporters Wednesday on Parliament Hill that she thought the special mediator’s value had been glossed over in the C-39 debate. The mediator is automatically engaged in situations where negotiations have broken down in the past, and works proactively to bring parties together between bargaining periods.

Hynes agreed that public pressure from a special mediator could help keep parties at the bargaining table and reduce the frequency of government intervention.

But he said he would like to see C-39’s proposed changes go further by giving the minister the power to head off a strike entirely in the rare instances when the economic stakes are high enough.

“If there’s a special mediator’s report that indicates … meaningful collective bargaining appears unlikely in this situation, we believe it’s perfectly reasonable in those situations for the minister to intervene in a pre-emptive manner before a catastrophic work stoppage is allowed to occur,” he said.

Vipond said she doesn’t believe that curtailing strikes can benefit the economy. She said Canada’s economy is healthiest when its workers have a seat at the table.

The Canadian Labour Congress met with MPs across party lines in recent weeks to make their case on Bill C-39. Vipond said the vast majority of those MPs were receptive to the group’s concerns but are ultimately falling along party lines.

Opposition parties have largely said they’ll vote against C-39, but the Liberals are expected to use their majority in the House of Commons to pass the proposed legislation through third reading. The bill would then proceed to the Senate for another round of scrutiny and possible amendments.

Vipond criticized the rapid pace of the House committee study, saying it failed to give MPs and staff enough time to process the labour community’s concerns. The labour congress will continue its outreach with senators in a bid to get its amendments adopted, but she expressed similar concerns about a possible time crunch in the Red Chamber.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 26, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Elon Musk is trying to build public support for his satellite and AI businesses during a period of intense public and political scrutiny of the tech space.
items.body:
Elon Musk plans to gift every child in the United States two SpaceX shares, as he attempts to build public support for his satellite and AI businesses during a period of intense public and political scrutiny of the technology sector.

The world’s richest person announced the share giveaway, which is worth a total of around US$18 billion, on the eve of U.S. Thanksgiving and just hours after SpaceX won U.S. approval on Wednesday to deploy one million satellites for data centers in space.

Musk is seeking to expand SpaceX’s role in the AI industry, even as the rapid growth of computing infrastructure raises concern about its environmental impact and the economic and political influence of technology billionaires.

Opponents of data centre development were among the biggest winners for the Democrats in this month’s US midterm elections.

“The initiative clearly helps broaden public participation in the SpaceX story,” Chez Anbu, head of wealth advisory at OCBC in Singapore, said on Thursday.

“Giving children a direct economic stake in the company creates a powerful narrative around broader participation in the benefits of the AI and space economy,” Anbu added.

The Federal Communications Commission said it approved SpaceX’s satellite constellation proposal to help meet rapidly growing demand for AI computing.

Astronomers have long been concerned about such developments in space and the American Astronomical Society said it was “disheartened and dismayed” by the FCC’s decision.

It warned the proposed constellation would “significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities” and the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky.

Share giveaway

Children would receive one share from SpaceX and one from him personally, Musk said in a post on X.

In a separate post on Thursday, Musk said he would continue the program in future years.

“I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year,” Musk wrote.

Musk earlier in the day said the SpaceX company shares would be transferred next month.

“The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year,” Musk added.

SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk would personally match the number of shares donated by the company.

A Trump Account is a program designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at US$127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly US$18 billion.

SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment on whether Musk’s SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.

“What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base,” said Christopher Brankin, global markets adviser at brokerage Mitrade Group.

“It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age,” he added.

Musk, whose net worth is around US$824 billion, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.

“Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many,” Musk said in a post on X at the time.

“Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way,” said Musk, most of whose philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than US$14 billion in assets.

SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell and her husband in October pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than two million children under the Trump initiative.

Musk and AI rival Anthropic have sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom.

Anthropic, which went public earlier this month, said in October that it was committing five per cent of its shares to a new fund for the “public good.”

Anthropic said its initiative, worth around US$54 billion at current prices, would give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity.

“It’s likely publicity for the Trump accounts... and also a counter to the Anthropic philanthropy noise that is likely to emerge,” said Mark Tinker, chief investment officer at Toscafund HK in Hong Kong.

“It is, after all, Thanksgiving!” Tinker added.

(Reporting by Gnaneshwar Rajan in Bengaluru, Tom Westbrook and Gregor Stuart Hunter, additional reporting by Neil J Kanatt; Writing by Miyoung Kim; Editing by Sonia Cheema, Lincoln Feast, Kate Mayberry and Alexander Smith)

items.title: EU leaders split over budget spending and a US$49 billion loan to Ukraine
items.description: European Union leaders struggled to bridge major differences over the bloc’s long-term budget and agree a new US$49 billion loan to help Ukraine.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[French President Emmanuel Macron speaks during a media conference at the EU summit in Brussels, Thursday, Nov. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Marius Burgelman)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Marius Burgelman</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: European Union leaders struggled to bridge major differences over the bloc’s long-term budget and agree a new US$49 billion loan to help Ukraine.
items.body:
BRUSSELS — French President Emmanuel Macron set an end-of-year deadline for an agreement on the European Union’s next seven-year budget after the continent’s leaders ruled out any chances for a deal to be reached at their summit on Thursday.

The 2028-2034 budget — a statement on broader EU ambitions — is small, compared to national budgets, and it is financed mostly by the 27 member countries based on the size of their economies. It is likely to amount to between 1 per cent and 1.2 per cent of the EU’s average gross national income.

At the bloc headquarters in Brussels on Thursday, EU leaders failed to reach a consensus after more than 12 hours of talks over the budget and a new US$49 billion loan for Ukraine’s economic and military needs next year.

  • Latest updates on international news here

Macron, whose country is mired in debt and faces elections in April that the hard right appears likely to win, ruled out any chance of immediate agreement. He said he would be ready to sign up to “a good agreement” when the leaders meet again on Dec. 17-18.

He said that after Dec. 31, he wouldn’t “be able to relaunch a discussion on the budget and to conclude it” as it would be “much too close to the presidential elections in France.”

Earlier, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar took to social media to say that he had seen “zero results” on Thursday and suggested that an agreement by “Christmas looks unlikely too.”

Smaller than national budgets but still plenty to argue over

During the talks, some European leaders called for belts to be tightened, while others defended traditional policies that consume large parts of the budget. Most want extra funds for important new priorities, and to help Ukraine almost five years into the war.

“Europe needs solid finances. We can’t and we mustn’t take on more debt,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, in remarks that highlighted some of the contradictions. “At the same time there is a series of tasks we must fulfill reliably.”

Germany is one of an important group of so-called net contributors that pay more into the budget than they get back in allocations, along with Austria, the Netherlands and Sweden, among others.

“The budget needs to be modernized and needs to be downsized if we want to strike a deal,” Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said. “I’m ready for this marathon, if it ends today, tomorrow or somewhere in December.”

Defending farm subsidies and infrastructure funds

A large group of countries, led by France and Italy and dubbed the “friends of cohesion,” staunchly defends funds that protect farmers and pay for infrastructure projects in relatively poor member countries, to help bring them up to EU standards.

Agriculture and cohesion policy each make up about a third of the budget.

“Cohesion is about the same level of life in different regions,” said Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, a billionaire. “We don’t have any highway to Austria, unfortunately, and we have to build our hospitals.”

European Council President António Costa, who is chairing a summit that could run into Friday, called on the leaders to approach the debate with an “open mind, a constructive approach and the sense of compromise.”

He said that an agreement is needed “by the end of this year, and for this, we need to reach unanimity.” Costa wants to secure agreement on the budget’s size, how to distribute funds between its priorities, and on ways to raise money from elsewhere.

Last week, he suggested an EU-wide tax on digital services. It would be drawn from online advertising and money that companies make from user data and could amount to 5 billion euros (US$5.5 billion) a year.

Ukraine and Europe’s budget conundrum

Ukraine is a big part of the budget puzzle. The spending package foresees a 100-billion-euro (US$110-billion) envelope for the government in Kyiv over seven years. The leaders must also decide on the new loan, and whether the costs of servicing it should be drawn from the budget.

Earlier this month, Merz threatened to hold up a budget agreement if there were no “collective commitment” made to Ukraine by all member countries, “without exception.”

Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia oppose using funds for military aid to Ukraine. Merz repeated his warning on Thursday and said that “we will talk about this in depth in one-on-one talks.”

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

But Babiš insisted that the “financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately,” and that the priority for Europe must be the “life of our citizens.”

Nearly a year ago, EU leaders endorsed a loan of 90 billion euros (US$99 billion) to cover most of the Ukrainian government’s needs for two years. But Russia’s intensified attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, along with disruptions to Black Sea trade, are straining Ukraine’s finances.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the EU’s plans to allocate money for Ukraine in its budget would make Kyiv “less inclined toward a peace process and more determined to continue the war.”

Lorne Cook, The Associated Press

The post Canadian Mortgage Delinquencies Rise, Led By Bigger Loans: TransUnion appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian mortgage delinquencies are climbing, led by larger loans. With rate relief off the table, TransUnion warns 2027 renewals risk amplifying stress.
items.body:
The Canadian real estate industry got more bad news this week, this time on the mortgage front. TransUnion data shows that mortgage credit grew in Q3 2026, but with fewer borrowers. Larger loans are driving the trend, with the biggest balances disproportionately fueling delinquencies. Now with rate relief off the table in 2027, lenders are bracing for things to get worse before they improve.

Fewer Mortgage Borrowers, Bigger Loans

Canadian mortgage debt is hitting new highs, despite fewer households carrying a mortgage. TransUnion data shows mortgage balances hit $1.96 trillion in Q3 2026, up 3.4% from last year. The balance represents 74% of the record $2.66 trillion in household debt reported to the bureau. However, active mortgage accounts slipped 0.5% to 6.6 million, while total mortgage holders fell 0.4% to 8.6 million.

That means the balance is growing due to larger mortgages, not more homeowners. The average mortgage balance hit $296,979, 3.9% higher than last year. New originations in Q2 (latest) drove the trend, averaging $374,562, up 4.2% from last year. Mortgage debt is concentrating around existing owners, not a broad expansion of ownership as seen in healthy markets.

Bigger Balances Lead Mortgage Delinquencies, Borrowers Tap Equity

More mortgage borrowers are cracking, according to the bureau’s data. The 60+ day delinquency rate climbed 4 basis points (bps) from last year to 0.31% of accounts and 0.33% of mortgage holders. The share of delinquent balances also climbed 6 bps over the period to 0.33%, outpacing both. The gap suggests that larger mortgages are disproportionately driving the delinquency trend.

Rising delinquencies won’t be calming soon, as there’s significant pressure building. Across all credit products, early 30+ day delinquencies fell to 4.3%, 6 bps lower than last year. However, the 60+ and 90+ day arrears both rose 3 bps to 2.6% and 1.8%, respectively. Fewer newly missed payments is good news, but borrowers who do fall behind are increasingly getting stuck.

Meanwhile, homeowners are leveraging their homes for more variable-rate debt—on top of their mortgages. Total line of credit balances rose 5.8% from last year to $300.8 billion, while new limits surged to an average of $92,489 in Q2 (latest), up 14.7% from last year. TransUnion specifically notes that this is driven heavily by what it calls “likely secured lending” above $80,000.

Collision Course With 2027 Renewals

TransUnion warns the biggest threat is upcoming mortgage renewals, not today’s delinquencies. Borrowers are set to renew with much bigger balances than in previous years, and many at higher rates. Newer originations with larger balances face far greater sensitivity to payment increases. The bureau notes that renewals won’t initiate mortgage deterioration—they risk amplifying existing stress.

That collision is happening just as rate relief has vanished. The Bank of Canada (BoC) hiked its policy rate 25 bps to 2.50% in October—its first increase since 2023. Both RBC and BMO are forecasting another rate hike in December, following a hawkish speech from the BoC governor this week. RBC and Scotiabank now project rates will climb as high as 3.25% in 2027. Lenders will be watching closely to see if higher renewal rates accelerate delinquencies.

items.title: Canadian Mortgage Awards: All the winner reaction from a landmark night
items.description: Winners from the CMAs' 20th anniversary share their thoughts on a memorable occasion in Toronto
items.content: <p>Winners from the CMAs' 20th anniversary share their thoughts on a memorable occasion in Toronto</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639313046166075122.jpeg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Winners from the CMAs' 20th anniversary share their thoughts on a memorable occasion in Toronto
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) marked their 20th anniversary on Wednesday evening with a landmark gala at Rebel Toronto, as hundreds of mortgage professionals gathered to celebrate the industry's top performers across 25 award categories.

From broker of the year honours to lifetime achievement recognition, the milestone event brought together some of Canada's most prominent lending professionals for a night that highlighted both the industry's resilience and its depth of talent.

Brokers in the spotlight

Rakhee Dhingra of Mortgage Savvy claimed two of the night's most coveted prizes, winning Broker of the Year for Regional, Eastern Canada (Quebec and Ontario) and, later in the evening, the CIMBC Award for Canadian Broker of the Year – the top individual broker honour of the night.

"I've absolutely enjoyed every moment of being in this industry, the learning, the challenges, the ups and the downs," she said after collecting the Eastern Canada award. "The fact that I get to wake up every day and do something I'm passionate about but still impact people's lives in such a meaningful way is such a gift."

Dhingra said her approach to the job is centred around connecting clients with their broader life goals. "It's about guiding clients through understanding how to use their mortgage to build the life they want to live," she said. "Being consistent, focusing on credibility, integrity, and trust, building a system and controls so you can continue to nurture those relationships — that's key."

After claiming the national honour, Dhingra offered profound words for industry members starting their career journey: "We have such a blessed opportunity to impact and create change, but also to create incredible lives for our families."

David Clarke of TMG The Mortgage Group won the Canadian Mortgages Inc. Award for Broker of the Year – Private Lending, an honour he had been nominated for before but had not yet collected. "I'm pretty excited about it," he said.

Clarke said a disciplined, data-driven approach had been essential throughout his year. "I figured out the amount of activities you've got to do to hit a certain result, and I just really follow the math of it."

His edge, he said, comes from building plans around realistic client behaviour: "I think sometimes plans are based off of somebody doing a complete 180, and I just don't think that works for most people. If somebody already spends their credit cards, there's a good chance they're going to again. You've got to build a plan that has the human in it."

Parminder Bhatti of AKAL Mortgages Inc. claimed the EQ Bank Award for Broker of the Year – Reverse Mortgages, winning a category introduced to the CMAs for the first time this year.

"I've been working with seniors for the last six years," said Bhatti, who dedicated the win to mentors he credited with inspiring his work in the reverse mortgage space. "It's a great time to have this category introduced."

Stephen Thomas of Mortgage Alliance HALO Mortgage Advisory took home the Grechi Carter Professional Corporation Award for Broker of the Year – Commercial, crediting an advice-first philosophy for his success.

"It's really just sticking to my purpose, which is providing advice to my borrowers," he said. "Whether I'm able to provide a solution or not, I can still provide advice to save people time and energy and effort and stress."

For Thomas, consistency is the strategy: "A lot of brokers will try to just fit a square peg into a round hole. If you can just keep advice and be efficient, you can save people a lot of stress and give them options."

Lending excellence recognised

Ronelle Landicho of Glasslake Funding claimed the Lender Underwriter of the Year award in the Specialist, Alternative and Private category for the second time, calling it a moment that never loses its impact.

"It's my second time winning, but it just never gets old. It feels like the first time," he said.

Landicho said the past year brought exceptional growth, with volume at Glasslake more than doubling year-over-year by his estimate. That’s a rise he attributed to his emphasis on building broker trust alongside technical underwriting skill. "I have a lot of deals that come in with brokers specifically asking me to underwrite their deals," he said. "People just think it's underwriting, but there's a lot of sales into it. You've got to sell yourself. You've got to build those relationships to gain the trust."

Laura Aiken, a senior underwriter at MCAP, won the Prime Lender Underwriter of the Year award with a broker-first approach and turnaround focus central to her success — especially in a year where rate competitiveness was not always assured.

"Even though our rates haven't always been there, know that my support is," she said. "I'm always just trying to get back to them as quickly as possible so that they know they'll have the best experience if they send their deals to us."

Cam Dellipizzi of MCAN Home Mortgage Group won Lender BDM of the Year in the Prime category and described the moment as a symbolic one for his career: he first attended the CMAs in 2012 as a Rookie of the Year winner, sitting at a table in the furthest corner of the venue from the stage.

"Tonight is like this full circle," he said. "I've done this job now since 2012 and I still don't get tired of working for the brokers."

He said his formula has not changed since then. "I pick up my phone, I answer my texts, I answer my emails. And I do pick up the phone at 5:00 on a Friday, and I take a lot of pride in that. It's all about relationship, being there for them when they need you."

Jerry Wieliczko of Hosper Mortgage was recognised as Lender BDM of the Year in the Specialist – Alternative and Private category after multiple nominations over the years.

"I'm very surprised. I never expected it," he said. "It was my eighth or ninth nomination, and finally I won." Wieliczko said his focus through a challenging housing market remained constant: "I'm always trying to help brokers wherever I can – to be wherever they need me."

Swish Goswami, CEO and co-founder of BrokerPlus, accepted the Industry Service Provider of the Year award for a company that had not yet reached its first anniversary — crediting the speed of the win to a philosophy built around listening to brokers.

"We started the company in March. It hasn't actually even been a year for us yet," said Goswami. "Some of the other companies in our space have forgotten sometimes that the brokers are really the people that you need to serve – and when I say serve, I don't just mean provide them something, I mean improve on it every day. Don't be satisfied by a product that you released in 2015 that was novel for its time."

Brokerages, teams, and networks

Clinton Wilkins of CENTUM Home Lenders in Halifax took home the Brokerage of the Year award for companies with fewer than 25 employees, bringing what he described as a point of regional pride back to Atlantic Canada.

"We have 10 brokers and the average broker on our team is doing over $50 million a year," said Wilkins. He attributed the team's success to a culture of education and client support: "Some of our secret sauce is really around education and really supporting our clients and our business partners — building a culture of success."

Wilkins also framed the win as a statement about his market. "Bringing the award home to Halifax and Atlantic Canada really puts us on the map and that we can compete with the big boys in Toronto and Vancouver."

Meaghan Hastings of The Mortgage Coach won the Brokerage/Team of the Year award for companies with 25 employees or more, crediting an investment in existing talent over new recruitment as the firm's key differentiator.

"We make a point of actually not focusing all of our efforts on recruitment," she said. "We really invest a lot in our agents and making sure that they are constantly improving, and hopefully that also improves us."

PMT Mortgage Corporation, led by Paul Meredith, was named New Brokerage of the Year. The team has operated for a decade but became an independent brokerage in 2024, Meredith said, making the award a significant milestone.

"It was hard not to get emotional up there," he said. "The biggest thing is that I've got a dream team that I put together." Meredith said the firm's success is rooted in a shared commitment to client experience. "We believe in building relationships with everybody, with all of our clients, and the entire team is right on board with that."

Dino DiPancrazio of M3 Financial Group accepted the Tru Cooperative Bank Award for National Brokerage of the Year on behalf of Mortgage Alliance, a multiple-time winner of the award. That’s a run he attributed to a broker-first philosophy and a growing investment in technology.

"Our motto for Mortgage Alliance is broker first always, and that is what we do," he said. "That's when the brokers need most support – in difficult times."

Rich Spence, president of Mortgage Centre Canada, accepted the National Broker Network of the Year award as a recognition of the more than 3,000 mortgage brokers his network represents across Canada.

"This really is for them," said Spence. "It's a network of individuals, entrepreneurs, lender partners, suppliers, and it's a great win for all of them." Spence said steady retention and ongoing recruitment underpin the network's growth.

Joel Wolodarsky and Shauna Clarke of IG Wealth Management accepted the Mortgage Industry Employer of Choice award for a firm that they said approaches mortgage advice through the lens of holistic financial planning.

"It takes building a star team because the mortgage business is really complex," said Wolodarsky. Clarke added that the firm's broader philosophy shapes the mortgage offering: "Our firm is focused on financial planning, and we provide mortgage advice in the context of a wider financial plan and reaching all of our clients' financial goals."

Innovation, community, and distinction

Dave Teixeira of DLCG won the Innovator Champion of the Year award, an honour he accepted as validation of a philosophy he has championed across the industry: build technology, then share it freely.

Among the tools Teixeira highlighted was an anti-money laundering risk rating tool released to the entire industry, which had seen more than 200,000 uses, according to Teixeira. "My overall philosophy on technology is it should be used to enhance lives, but then let's share it as far and wide as we can," he said. "In the age of AI, it's even easier to build – the barrier to entry is smaller, it democratises what we're doing."

Teixeira also spoke to the broader meaning of the category. "It's great to see that the industry is recognising that innovation is what's going to take us to the next step," he said. "How do we get from the industry that we've known to the industry that we could become?"

Dalia Barsoum, founder of Streetwise Mortgages/Streetwise Wealth, was named Finfluencer of the Year – a category introduced by REMIC recognising financial education delivered to Canadians through social media and digital channels.

Barsoum said her YouTube channel grew organically by responding to the questions her clients were raising. "With the market shift, people are having more and more questions about renewals, about private mortgages, about challenges we've never experienced before," she said. "I decided: I'm just going to talk about these things from a solution standpoint."

"For me, it's not about the clicks," Barsoum said. "It's really about putting out content that really makes a difference — content that informs, that people can remember and engage with. It just grew organically because what we're delivering, people saw value in."

Frances Hinojosa of Tribe was named Woman of Distinction, a recognition she described in terms of the generational shift she has witnessed over 30 years in finance.

"Thirty years ago, there were more suits in the boardroom than there were skirts," she said. "To be in finance and stick it out that long, to turn around and win the Women of Distinction – to me it's an honour to show the visibility to the next generation that it is possible for you to progress in anything that you want to do in your career moving forward."

Hinojosa offered advice for those starting out in their mortgage industry career: "Just keep going. Speak your mind. Be yourself. You think that you don't matter, but the little things will always matter the most in business."

Emily Kiparisas of SafeBridge Financial Group was named Young Achiever of the Year, an honour she described as "shocking" but deeply meaningful.

"I'm just really focusing on creating a different experience for a client and making them feel seen, recognised, understanding their life goals," said Kiparisas. She was quick to credit her team, describing them as integral to her work. "Without them, I wouldn't be where I am today."

Hugo Neveu and Jean-Francois Jacquet of CONSORTIUM Hypothécaire accepted the RFA Award for Excellence in Philanthropy and Community Service, dedicating the recognition to the causes – and the people behind them – that the firm supports.

The organisation has been a key backer of Strike Out Cancer, including helping to bring the initiative to Quebec City for the first time last year. "We try to do our best to support people in our community, especially children in need," the recipients said. "As an industry, we need to give back to everyone as soon as we can."

A milestone for the industry

Few awards at this year's ceremony carried as much weight as the Lifetime Achievement honour, presented to Jason Ellis of First National Financial LP – a recognition that also served as a fitting symbol for the CMAs' own 20-year journey.

"It's surreal, and I would say imposter syndrome taken to the next level," Ellis said. "I'm proud of a lot of what we accomplished together at First National, but I feel like I was just part of a team. Careers are built on teams. It's not really an individual thing."

Ellis acknowledged the individuals whose foundations he built upon: First National co-founders Stephen Smith and Maury Taws, and long-serving colleague Scott McKenzie. "I'm only here because of all of the people at First National. The sum of the parts much greater than the person."

Sponsors and closing

The evening was made possible by an impressive roster of sponsors: event partner the Coalition of Independent Mortgage Brokers of Canada (CIMBC), EQ Bank, Haventree Bank, Canadian Mortgages Inc. (CMI), MCAN, the Real Estate and Mortgage Institute of Canada (REMIC), Grechi Carter Professional Corporation, Real Property Solutions (RPS), RFA Financial, Tru Cooperative Bank, OIM Group, Bank of Montreal (BMO), HomeEquity Bank, and M3 Financial.

CMP extends its congratulations to all 25 category winners and its thanks to everyone who attended Wednesday night's celebration – and to all those who make the Canadian Mortgage Awards possible year after year.

items.title: GTA New Home Sales Post Best October In 3 Years As HST Rebate Deadline Nears
items.description:
New home sales in the Greater Toronto Area had their strongest October in three years, according to the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD).

There were 1,340 new home sales in October, up significantly from October 2025, according to Altus Group, BILD's official source for new home market data. That's still 51% below the 10-year average of 2,729 sales for the month.

BILD credits the HST rebate program, saying buyers are using the savings to shift toward more attainable homes like townhomes and stacked townhouses.

The expanded rebate removes the full 13% HST for eligible buyers of new homes priced up to $1 million, for a maximum rebate of $130,000. It runs until March 31, 2027.

Low-rise homes led the way. There were 958 low-rise sales in October, a significant increase from a year ago and 21% above the 10-year average. Low-rise includes detached, linked, and semi-detached houses and townhouses (excluding stacked townhouses).

High-rise homes, which include units in low-, medium-, and high-rise buildings and stacked townhouses, accounted for 382 sales, 80% below the 10-year average.

"GTA new home sales in October posted another strong showing thanks in large part to the HST rebate program. This month we saw the high-rise sector join the upswing with stacked townhouses hitting a nearly five-year high," said Edward Jegg, Research Manager at Altus Group. "Stacked townhouses offer more space than a condominium apartment and the HST rebate dramatically aids with the affordability crunch buyers are facing."

The benchmark price for a new low-rise home was $1,259,190, down 12.2% over the last 12 months. The benchmark price for a new high-rise unit was $1,053,085, up 2% from last year.

Both are gross prices that don't reflect the HST rebate. BILD reports them this way so they can be compared directly with previous years; buyers who qualify for the rebate would see additional savings.

Total remaining inventory in the GTA fell to 19,202 units. Low-rise inventory rose to 7,504 homes, or 11 months of inventory. High-rise inventory fell to 11,698 units, or about 44 months of inventory, based on average sales over the last 12 months.

In Simcoe County, there were 73 low-rise new home sales and no high-rise sales in October. The weighted average price of those low-rise homes was $968,212.

BILD is pushing the federal and provincial governments to extend the rebate before it expires.

"To date, there have been nearly 9,000 families in the province who have achieved new home ownership because of the HST rebate program. It also has supported nearly 34,000 industry jobs and stimulated $5 billion in economic activity and nearly $2 billion in provincial and municipal revenue," said Justin Sherwood, Chief Operating Officer at BILD.

"With the program set to expire on March 31, 2027, it would be incredibly impractical of the federal and provincial governments to not extend a program that is the sole bright spot of a very bleak housing picture."

items._ogDesc: Governor Tiff Macklem’s hawkish speech has BMO calling for a December rate hike to 2.75%, right as the Bank of Canada revives its old CPIX measure
items.body:
Canada’s central bank wasn’t discussing rate hikes, but it left a loud and clear message. Bank of Canada (BoC) Governor Tiff Macklem delivered a hawkish speech in Toronto this week, all but confirming rate hikes. BMO Capital Markets now expects the BoC to hike its key policy rate at its December meeting, after the Governor stated the economy no longer needs stimulus.

Bank of Canada Expected To Hike In December, Says BMO

After the latest comments from the BoC Governor, BMO sees a 25-basis-point hike in December. That would leave the policy rate at 2.75%, the mid-point of the neutral policy range, where monetary policy neither provides stimulus nor becomes restrictive. The hawkish tone appears to have surprised BMO, which noted the Governor didn’t address any economic weakness.

“Governor Macklem’s speech in Toronto reinforced the Bank of Canada’s recent hawkish messaging. He omitted any mention of the recent run of soft data, and reiterated worries about spillover from above-target headline inflation,” explains Benjamin Reitzes, BMO’s Canadian Rates & Macro Strategist. “One key rationale noted is that the economy no longer needs policy in stimulative territory.”

Bank of Canada Returns To Old Inflation Measure

Despite the finance industry taking away enough to update forecasts, the speech wasn’t meant to set expectations—at least not directly, notes BMO.

“The focus of the speech was the renewal of the inflation targeting framework, and the Governor unveiled that the Bank’s preferred core measures are now CPI-Trim and CPIX,” explains Reitzes.

Neither is a new core measure, but they’re not the headline numbers the media leads with. CPI-Trim seeks to strip out the extremes of the basket, eliminating the top and bottom 20% of price movements. It sounds like that would be a fair trade-off, but in reality, upward price pressure tends to be more extreme than downward. As a result, big price jumps are filtered out with much smaller relative moves downward.

The Governor clarified, however, that these measures will be used in addition to the headline CPI. “Mr. Macklem stressed that the 2% inflation target applies exclusively to headline CPI. The cores will be used as a guide to forecast where overall inflation is headed,” explains Reitzes.


As for CPIX, it stands for Consumer Price Index eXcluding, as it excludes the 8 most volatile components and the effects of indirect tax changes. It’s an oldie that was introduced in 2001, but dropped in 2016 in favour of three core measures—CPI-trim, CPI-median, and CPI-common. A good reminder that sometimes policymakers control inflation, and sometimes they control how it’s measured.

items.content: <p>BMO projects 2% growth for Canada in 2027 as housing markets brace for further rate jumps</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312262342042131.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: BMO projects 2% growth for Canada in 2027 as housing markets brace for further rate jumps
items.body:
Canada's mortgage markets are heading into 2027 facing at least one more Bank of Canada rate hike, as BMO Capital Markets upgrades its national growth forecast to 2% while identifying British Columbia and Ontario as the provinces most exposed to continued monetary tightening.

The November 24 report by Douglas Porter, CFA, Managing Director and Chief Economist at BMO Capital Markets in Toronto, and Robert Kavcic, Director and Senior Economist at BMO Capital Markets, projects Canada's gross domestic product (GDP) above the 20-year average in 2027.

That follows an estimated 1% expansion in 2026, weighed down by US tariffs of 50% on steel and aluminum and 35% on lumber, with no significant trade resolution assumed in the base case.

"If we do get some kind of arrangement with the US, some certainty, some clarity on trade with the US, I would be much, much more optimistic in 2027, and I think we could grow well above average if we were to get some kind of an arrangement on trade," he said at the event.

On monetary policy, he was equally direct.

"We do believe that the Bank of Canada is likely to hike rates one more time," Porter said. "Our view is that two rate hikes will be enough."

Central banks globally raised rates this year as oil prices drove inflation higher, and Porter flagged that energy product prices — particularly diesel and heating oil — had not yet fully passed through to consumers.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem already signalled the risk of a second-round oil shock and rising December rate odds.

The rate outlook is the most pressing near-term concern for mortgage professionals. Porter outlined the dual pressure on households in a March interview with Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"It's not good. On the one side, there's the hit to confidence because of the uncertainty for the outlook and the very real hit to people's pocketbooks from higher gasoline prices," he said.

"At the same time, we've had this backup in long-term bond yields, which is threatening to push up longer-term mortgage rates. It's tough for the housing market on both fronts."

Experts from the Bank of Canada, Dominion Lending Centres (DLC), and TD Economics say higher rates and inflation remain key factors shaping the outlook for borrowers and the mortgage market in 2027. https://t.co/SP0gdfkLH5 — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 23, 2026

Ontario and BC most exposed to further rate hikes

The regional implications for mortgage professionals are significant. Kavcic identified British Columbia and Ontario as the provinces most vulnerable to continued tightening.

"Any upward pressure on mortgage rates would further deter buyers and slow construction activity, delaying a recovery in those markets," he noted in the report, citing elevated household debt and prolonged housing downturns in both provinces.

Ontario prices remain in retreat in some markets and construction has pulled back sharply; BC has endured a multi-year slump.

Regional divide deepens as prairies outperform

Alberta and Saskatchewan are delivering the country's strongest results, backed by elevated oil revenues and minimal US tariff exposure.

An influx of interprovincial residents has reinforced Alberta's consumer spending and residential demand.

Atlantic Canada is also above the national average, driven by migration and public infrastructure investment.

Quebec faces the steepest tariff headwinds, its aluminum sector absorbing a disproportionate share of US trade measures, compounded by its sensitivity to energy price volatility as a manufacturing base.

On the federal budget, Porter was clear about Ottawa's intent. 

"Their priority is really not on reducing the budget deficit — it is on supporting the Canadian economy through this difficult episode of trade uncertainty with the US," he said.

The projected $62.3 billion deficit for the 2026–2027 fiscal year arrives in line with expectations, and BMO estimates that defence and infrastructure commitments could add up to $150 billion to the economy over five years, with domestic suppliers prioritised.
