items.content: <p>High debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312227283291504.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: High debt and rising delinquency signal growing strain for 2027 mortgage renewals
items.body:
Canadian households entered the fourth quarter of 2026 carrying record consumer debt, with mounting pressure emerging among mortgage borrowers ahead of what is forecast to be a large renewal year in 2027, according to TransUnion Canada's Q3 2026 Credit Industry Insights Report (CIIR).

Total outstanding consumer credit debt reached $2.66 trillion in Q3 2026, up 3.8% year-over-year. The average Canadian owed $136,024 across all credit products, a 2.9% annual increase.

Mortgages represent 74% of outstanding balances, while non-mortgage debt – including credit cards, auto loans, and lines of credit – grew fastest at 3.6% year-over-year to an average of $28,083 per consumer.

Consumers in the super prime (lowest-risk) credit tier increased 4% year-over-year and represented nearly half of all scored credit-active Canadians.

Bigger balances, not more borrowers

Mortgage debt growth in Q3 2026 was not driven by an expanding pool of borrowers. Between September 2024 and September 2026, the average mortgage balance per consumer rose 8.6%, from $369,658 to $401,509, while the count of active mortgage holders grew by less than 1%.

While delinquency remains below pre-pandemic levels, the concentration of debt in larger individual balances is amplifying the financial stakes at renewal.

Matt Fabian, senior director of financial services research and consulting at TransUnion Canada, said lenders should closely track the divergence.

"Rising debt is being driven by two distinct forces: non-mortgage balance growth has come from an increase in borrowers carrying moderately higher average debt levels, while mortgage balance growth has come from larger balances per borrower as borrower counts have remained flat," Fabian said.

"For lenders, these differing patterns underscore the value of tracking how balances, product mix and payment obligations change over time."

Shaun Cathcart and Garry Bhaura of CREA, Michael Davenport of Oxford Economics, and Sherry Cooper of Dominion Lending Centres Group say higher rates and economic uncertainty are keeping Canada's housing market subdued. https://t.co/3C37E4W4gQ — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 18, 2026

Delinquency creep ahead of 2027 renewals

Mortgage delinquency trended upward across all stages in Q3 2026, with balance-level delinquency rising 6 basis points year-over-year and serious delinquency (90-plus days) outpacing account-level increases. That means larger-balance loans are overrepresented among distressed borrowers.

Victor Tran, Rates.ca mortgage and real estate expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year that mortgage arrears remain far from crisis territory.

"But I think it's going to be a slow grind," Tran said. "It's not going to be a significant, drastic increase suddenly and I don't think we're going to see sudden mass foreclosures or power of sales."

On October 28, the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%, its first rate increase since July 2023, adding immediate upward pressure on adjustable-rate mortgages and complicating renewal calculations across a broad segment of the market. 

Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, said that financial pressure on homeowners is real even in the absence of a default crisis.

"Mortgage delinquency is often one of the last signs of financial strain, because most homeowners will cut back in other areas before missing a mortgage payment," she said.

"That's why even a small increase in arrears is worth paying attention to. It can suggest that some households have already used savings, leaned on credit, or reduced everyday spending to keep up. For borrowers coming up for renewal, the question isn't only whether they can make the next payment, but whether payments can be sustained over time."

Fabian added that warning signals typically surface elsewhere in a consumer's finances before a mortgage payment is skipped.

"Rising utilization, growing revolving balances, reduced payments and emerging delinquency on other products can signal weakening financial capacity before a mortgage payment is missed," he said.

"Having a comprehensive view across the consumer wallet can reveal early signs of mortgage stress and give lenders an opportunity to identify risk earlier and engage consumers proactively."

items.title: Bank of Canada: Experts’ 2027 expectations for the central bank
items.description: Here's what could be in store from the BoC over the next 12 months
items.content: <p>Here's what could be in store from the BoC over the next 12 months</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639312227730594328.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Here's what could be in store from the BoC over the next 12 months
items.body:
The Bank of Canada still has one interest rate decision to go before the end of this year – but with 2027 just around the corner, plenty of attention among mortgage shoppers and industry members is turning to the central bank’s likely approach to rates over the next 12 months.

The BoC’s 25-basis-point rate hike on October 28 was its first increase since July 2023, and with inflation expected to rise further as the US-Iran war continues, most experts say the central bank isn’t likely to announce a prolonged pause on rate jumps again anytime soon.

Each of the major Canadian banks is continuing to monitor the economic outlook closely as they map out the Bank of Canada’s possible rate path for 2027.

  • Bank of Montreal (BMO) sees a Q1 2027 move to 2.75%, with the bank moving its rate-hike call forward to the BoC’s next decision on December 9 following hawkish remarks by Governor Tiff Macklem this week.
  • Scotiabank expects gradual rate hikes by the central bank through 2027, with the Bank then set to hold at 3.25% through 2028.
  • Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) projects a rate hike in December, rising to 3.25% and remaining at that level through 2028.
  • Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) expects rates to hit 2.75% by March and remain at that level through 2028.
  • National Bank is expecting rates to reach 2.75% by the first quarter and 3% by the second. It sees rates remaining at that level until at least the end of 2028.
  • Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD) expects the Bank of Canada’s overnight target rate to hit 2.75% in Q1, remaining at that level for the rest of the year and through 2028.

Why rates are likely to keep rising

The main reason Canada’s banking giants see the central bank keeping rate hikes on the table is no secret: that Iran war has pushed up oil prices and sparked concern about the inflation outlook, with Macklem and other global central bank governors noting the potential for more price pressures spilling into 2027.

Five-year Government of Canada bond yields, which strongly influence fixed mortgage rates, moved steadily higher in August and September as financial market expectations hardened around BoC rate hikes.

In October, the Bank of Canada’s 25-basis-point rate increase was accompanied by remarks suggesting more hikes could be on the way, although decisionmakers struck a careful tone on the economic outlook.

“There could be a need to increase the policy rate further,” the Bank’s statement read, “but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully.”

This week, Macklem warned that energy cost pressures still haven’t fully reached consumers, keeping a BoC December rate hike firmly in play and hinting that the central bank is expecting inflation to remain sticky into 2027.

What the Bank of Canada’s rate path means for borrowers

While the Bank is back in rate-hiking mode, experts don’t see a flurry of rate hikes similar to those witnessed in 2022 and 2023, when the central bank tackled rampant inflation by spiking its benchmark rate by 475 basis points.

Instead, the increases are likely to be milder – but that will still have implications for Canadian borrowers. Variable-rate holders without a fixed payment will see their costs rise with each additional hike, and those with renewals due in 2027 could find themselves in a higher rate environment than when they last signed.

Fixed-rate borrowers aren’t shielded either. Their rates don’t rise and fall in line with BoC decisions, but those five-year Government of Canada bond yields are an important driver of fixed rates – and they often move in expectation of central bank rate changes.

Economists and experts are keen to emphasize that much will depend on how political and economic factors play out in 2027. The inflation picture and outcomes of the US-Iran conflict and ongoing Canada-US trade war will likely have much to say on the BoC’s approach to rates next year.

For now, all eyes are on December 9 and the Bank’s language in its statement, one which could give a clearer indication of how the central bank is weighing the outlook for the months ahead.

items.description: MoneyBroker Canada’s Xu on navigating the 2026 market – and why the B side continues to grow
items.content: <p>MoneyBroker Canada’s Xu on navigating the 2026 market – and why the B side continues to grow</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639312226935243620.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: MoneyBroker Canada’s Xu on navigating the 2026 market – and why the B side continues to grow
items.body:
Alternative mortgage lending is continuing to grow as plenty of Canadians turn their attentions toward the sector amid affordability challenges and other hurdles. We caught up with MoneyBroker Canada founder Christine Xu to hear her thoughts on that growth and what’s next.

[00:00] This year is one of the most challenging years actually in my 26 years in the industry. The biggest challenge is there's no equity there. The price is almost 50% of the original condo purchase price. Within one day 30 spots filled.

[00:28] Fergal McAlinden: All right. So, next up in our interview series, we have Christine Xu, founder of Money Broker Canada. Really happy to have you with us today. First of all, how are things with you? How's the year been?

[00:38] Christine Xu: It's okay. This year is one of the most challenging years actually in my 26 years in the industry.

[00:44] Fergal McAlinden: What are some of the reasons that it's been such a challenge? We hear about affordability issues. Obviously, the market's slower, things like that. Is that the main issue?

[00:52] Christine Xu: Yeah. Combination of the whole thing. The market is getting very slow and we don't see the end of it and everybody is stressed, very stressed with the money and affordability issues.

[01:05] Fergal McAlinden: You're a seasoned professional in the industry and as you mentioned you've been in it for 26 years. How have you been approaching the market this year because it's challenging not just for borrowers but also for industry members. What's been your approach?

[01:16] Christine Xu: Lots of times basically we had to tell the client to face reality. In my business, our focus is alternative financing and lots of people coming to us just not enough equity in the properties and the income is not there.

[01:37] Not only we're not able to do the business, I'm turning businesses away. I say probably the only solution is selling the property. We try to be more creative to see whether there's other ways to help the problem. A lot of times if they have other properties, we bundle different properties together, try to think about other products with no income qualification requirement.

[01:59] So we do more private mortgages than even B lender mortgages. We haven't really seen too many people who qualify for the A side, but B side right now becomes the new A. The good thing is lots of new private lenders are more competitive with the B side too. So that's a good thing for the lower cost on the private side, but the biggest challenge is there's no equity there.

[02:30] Fergal McAlinden: Has the profile of the borrower type that you're dealing with changed a lot over the past few years with more people having to turn to private and alternative financing? Does that profile look a lot different?

[02:41] Christine Xu: Yeah. The profile is similar. I'm dealing with lots of self-employed people, new immigrant people, and that's why I focus more on the alternative side because income is not going to be enough.

[02:55] But the more challenging part is lots of those people are risky investors. They invest in a whole bunch of pre-construction condos and they are being hit the most. Lots of people who were doing great are now the most affected, like big-shot realtors. They bought so many pre-construction units themselves. Now we're seeing bankruptcy all over the place.

[03:20] Fergal McAlinden: The pre-construction condo story is one that we've all been talking about for years. Do you see any light at the end of the tunnel on that front? Is there still pain to go or what do you think is in store?

[03:31] Christine Xu: I think the market is being stable, but stable means the price is already low. It's already down so much. My son actually just bought a condo, closing by the end of this month. The price is almost 50% of the original condo purchase price.

[03:52] So the original owner walked away and gave the condo back to the builder. Luckily for him, as a first-time homebuyer getting into the market for a new construction condo, he gets the HST rebate, which is huge. He's getting a really good bargain.

[04:13] For people who actually need to buy real estate for their own use, I think that's really the best time to get into, even for condos too. But for investors, you have to be cautious with your cash flow.

[04:26] Fergal McAlinden: We've actually spoken with a few people today who have talked about opportunities for first-time buyers that maybe weren't there a couple of years ago. As you mentioned, the investor opportunities aren't really there, but on the plus side for first-time buyers like maybe your son, definitely a better outlook for them, right?

[04:41] Christine Xu: Right. And then also actually I've been really promoting reverse mortgages these days.

[04:47] Fergal McAlinden: Yeah?

[04:48] Christine Xu: So people like me who's trying to help my son, actually luckily he didn't need my help at all, but imagine lots of times parents want to help their children. Probably taking a reverse mortgage route is a very good route too.

[05:01] Fergal McAlinden: Is that a sector that you had transacted in a lot before or is it very new to you?

[05:05] Christine Xu: Reverse mortgages are gaining more market awareness now. I think because the baby boomer generation is getting older, they're really a perfect candidate for reverse mortgages. There's just not enough education out there.

[05:21] I was very surprised. I did my reverse mortgage seminar yesterday. It was the second time and each time it's overwhelming. We got like 30 people. That's our limit. The first time, within one day, 30 spots filled and yesterday the same thing. People were asking me to do some other sessions. I think the market awareness is getting there because we are aging already.

[05:50] Fergal McAlinden: Is there anything for agents and brokers transacting in that sector that you think is especially important to keep in mind about reverse mortgages?

[05:59] Christine Xu: Right. People who are dealing with the older generation, I think getting reverse mortgages is also a very good way to get in touch with the younger generation, which is going to be a big buying force in the market too.

[06:16] There are some younger Asians coming into the market and that's a good way to know their parents' generation. People taking reverse mortgages are not only taking the money. They could be buying another property for their children or for their own cash flow purposes.

[06:34] Fergal McAlinden: Well, a really interesting time for the market at the minute. How about events like this, Christine? Why are they important for you to attend or what do you think industry members can get out of events like this today?

[06:42] Christine Xu: I love to go to industry events. Every event I go to, I always learn something. New lenders, new lender product updates. I think for a new broker that's very important too. At least when you talk to a lender you can put a face together. Sometimes relationship also works.

[07:01] Fergal McAlinden: Great stuff. Just before I let you go, I wanted to ask about your thoughts for the next few months and looking ahead. We're almost at the end of 2026. What do you think about 2027? Is there more of the same in store or do you see trends shifting a little bit?

[07:14] Christine Xu: I think next year probably very similar to this year. We will see interest rates actually going higher and the long-term interest rate will definitely go higher because in the US it's already higher.

[07:30] So it doesn't really help the market, but hopefully we're more resilient and people are already getting used to this market. No matter what industry you are in, there are always people who are survivors and are doing well. I hope the audience are survivors.

[07:44] Fergal McAlinden: I know. Withstanding times like this just sets you in better stead for whenever things get better, right? You're kind of developing the skills that you need to succeed whenever the wave starts.

[07:55] Christine Xu: Yeah. Lots of times we're thinking about different revenue streams, thinking outside the box. I think the most important thing is marketing and getting clients. You've got to think about more creative ways to get clients, whether you're using AI, CRM systems, or doing in-person meetings.

[08:15] For me, I'm more in-person. I love to go to events. People here, you not only learn things, but they can be your very good partners in business too. Everybody you meet at events can be your potential client.

[08:30] Fergal McAlinden: One last question. You mentioned AI. There's a bit of a divide in terms of who's using it, who's not, who sees the benefit and who doesn't. How are you using it yourself in your work?

[08:40] Christine Xu: For myself, I think I'm more like one of the slowest adopters, but I'm using AI basically to ask questions, asking for thoughts. Sometimes simple things, like spelling. I say, how do you spell a word? But I think we'll learn to use more. Really, AI is the future.

[09:01] Fergal McAlinden: Brilliant. Well, thank you very much for your time and always great to talk to you.

[09:04] Christine Xu: Yeah, thanks. Thank you.

items.title: Brokers ‘not in the mortgage business – we’re in the people business’
items.description: Tribe Financial CEO Hinojosa talks the latest trends in mortgage
items.content: <p>Tribe Financial CEO Hinojosa talks the latest trends in mortgage</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639312224758288828.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tribe Financial CEO Hinojosa talks the latest trends in mortgage
items.body:
Tribe Financial chief executive officer Frances Hinojosa sat down with CMP at MortgageFest to discuss AI, a changing mortgage market, and why face-to-face connection still matters.

[00:00] We're not in the mortgage business. We truly are in the people business.

[00:14] Fergal McAlinden: All right, we're continuing our day two interviews for Mortgage Fest 2026. On stage with us now, we have Frances Hinojosa, CEO of Tribe Financial and also our chair for the event. You've been here wearing many hats. You're not just a chair. You've also been a participant. You've been a moderator. What are some of the main things you've been talking about over the past couple of days?

[00:33] Frances Hinojosa: A lot about AI and a lot about technology, which is not a surprise. You can see it all over the news these days. AI is coming. It's another pivotal change that's coming to our industry and the expansion that is coming. One of the themes I talked about even when I did the chair opening is that brokers and agents can't be scared of it. When advancements come, you got to figure out a way to embrace it as opposed to being left behind because there is a lot of great things that you can be using with this tool.

[01:00] I think shying away from it is the last thing you want to do in your business because you will be left behind at the end of the day.

[01:08] Fergal McAlinden: How are you using it yourself in your own business?

[01:10] Frances Hinojosa: Like basics, really basics. A lot of it using around research. A lot of it using around keeping myself more efficient, maintaining my notes. For me, the way that I treat AI in my own business is using it as a tool as though I had another assistant in my staff. Summarizing news reports. That was a great tip that was given today at the women's conference.

[01:33] Most of us as brokers, we get very busy and we're inundated with news every single day. Staying on top of policies, staying on top of the news, staying on economic data, AI is a great tool for that. Something as simple as ChatGPT. I can say give me the latest headlines as it pertains to my work or what the trends are going to be and I can get an itemized report. So I'm condensing down and creating more time in my day, as I like to say, to be more human and do other human-like activities and allocate that time accordingly.

[02:01] Fergal McAlinden: It seems to me that it's not really replacing a lot of the core functions of a broker. It's maybe helping out with some of the backend things and admin stuff, things like that, but your function as a broker is remaining unchanged.

[02:12] Frances Hinojosa: Absolutely. It's just enhancing it. I'll tell you a very quick story. I've been in finance for over 30 years. I remember when ATMs were brought to the bank branches. That's how far back I go.

[02:29] I remember when the first ATM was installed in one of the bank branches that I worked at. This is like three decades ago. The narrative was like, "Oh my God, it's going to replace all you people in the bank branches." Fast forward a couple years, that's when telephone banking or online banking got introduced. Same thing. It's going to replace all the people. It never replaced it. It enhanced it. It gives another option.

[02:54] It allows you to create more time to be more human. I think we can't fear technology. We have to embrace it in the way that works best for you and your business, but don't discount it because you're missing out on a lot of good things.

[02:55] Fergal McAlinden: How about the current market? That's a big topic of conversation. Obviously, lenders, brokers on your panel yesterday too. How are you viewing things at the minute?

[03:04] Frances Hinojosa: I think we are going through a pivotal time, but I'm a firm believer that anytime we're in a marketplace where there's great change, great disruption, or great challenges that come to us, it gives you an opportunity to reinvent yourself, to think where you can do things differently and where you can really enhance your business.

[03:22] Challenges aren't there to create disruption or prevent you from doing business. I believe it's a stopping point that's saying, "Hey, maybe what worked before won't work moving forward." At the end of the day, any challenges that come into a marketplace, this too shall pass. But are you going to be ready for the next stage, the next evolution?

[03:43] I feel we're at a time right now where things will change and evolution is coming in the marketplace. Are you going to be prepared and are you going to be evolving? Use this time right now instead of complaining or griping about how bad the market conditions are. Find the opportunities because there's always opportunities that are out there.

[04:00] Fergal McAlinden: Speaking of opportunities, it's got to be great as a broker to be able to speak with people face to face at events like these. We're usually doing interviews by phone or by Teams, but here we are face to face. So it's got to be good.

[04:13] Frances Hinojosa: It's great. That's one thing, too. I'm so happy to see so many brokers have come out, and I'm hoping that next year for Mortgage Fest, more of you come out to this event because I think it is super important.

[04:22] It re-energizes you having these conversations or sitting in with these different panels. You're picking up different little nuggets of stuff that you may not have known otherwise. And let's be honest, I talked about this in the opening address. We're not in the mortgage business. We truly are in the people business if you think about it. And it's about building relationships.

[04:42] You cannot build relationships if you're at home behind your computer day in and day out. You need to come to events like Mortgage Fest, meet other brokers, meet your lenders, meet your colleagues, and that is the way that you're going to elevate yourself and give you that little spark. We're energetic beings. We need that spark of energy.

[05:01] Fergal McAlinden: My last question was going to be if we're going to see you back here next year, but it sounds like we are.

[05:06] Frances Hinojosa: A thousand percent. I'm going to be back here next year, and I hope you're back here too. You have to come to Mortgage Fest next year. I really believe you guys have done a stellar job. This is a top-tier conference.

[05:17] Anyone thinking about it or missed out this year, you don't want to miss it next year. You definitely want to come back because I know Fergal, you guys and the team are going to make it bigger, better. It is something that you definitely do not want to miss.

[05:27] Fergal McAlinden: We sure are. And thanks to you for all your help with the event, as I said, all that you've done with us, chair, moderator, everything. We'll see you next year. Looking forward to it.

[05:34] Frances Hinojosa: See you next year. Thanks, Fergal.

items.description: Questbank’s Merdita on what’s next for a lender with big plans for the mortgage sector
items.content: <p>Questbank’s Merdita on what’s next for a lender with big plans for the mortgage sector</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639312222584068414.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Questbank’s Merdita on what’s next for a lender with big plans for the mortgage sector
items.body:
At MortgageFest, we spoke with QuestBank’s head of sales and marketing Bekim Merdita to hear about what’s next for the fast-growing lender – and its plans for the mortgage broker space.

[00:00] We really are building a bank before everyone else's eyes and we are Canada's newest bank and building it side by side with our broker partners.

[00:17] Fergal McAlinden: All right. Well, next up we have got Bekim Merdita, Head of Sales and Marketing newly at QuestBank. Bekim, first of all, congrats on the very recent role you've stepped into. How's it all been going so far?

[00:28] Bekim Merdita: It's a lot of fun. It's a whirlwind. It's good to be talking to you again. It's been a little while. Looks amazing in here first and foremost, but yeah, just having a lot of fun having great conversations with brokers again. It's what I love doing.

[00:39] Fergal McAlinden: Kind of familiar territory for you, obviously, speaking with the agents and brokers from across not just Ontario, but Canada too. What are some of the main messages that you want to get out today and some of the main things you'll be talking about with brokers?

[00:50] Bekim Merdita: I think the biggest thing that's new for us this year compared to times past, Community Trust, a 50-year-old trust company, at the end of last year got our banking license as a Schedule I bank and rebranded ourselves to QuestBank, which we're really excited about. It gives us the ability to not just do mortgage products, but other products as well that serve the consumer and really start building a financial ecosystem for our consumer.

[01:15] So, we're really excited about that. Having conversations with brokers about not just the mortgage but other products that we can carry. The way I like to think about it is we really are building a bank before everyone's eyes. You think about the other banks that have been around, most of them are hundreds of years old, and we are Canada's newest bank, building it side by side with our broker partners. That's a really exciting opportunity.

[01:37] Fergal McAlinden: It's cool because to a lot of people that sounds like a daunting challenge, but I know you've got that entrepreneurial mindset and background. It's got to be really exciting for you to take on that challenge.

[01:47] Bekim Merdita: I've been running startups for years, so to be now running a bank as a startup, it's an interesting twist. Most people don't put the two things together, but what an interesting opportunity. We're having fun.

[01:59] Fergal McAlinden: When you're speaking with brokers today, obviously it's a really interesting market that they're in. We know there's a lot of challenges, but opportunities too. How are you looking at the market at the minute? And what are some of those opportunities that brokers should be keeping their eye on?

[02:11] Bekim Merdita: I think some things change and some things stay the same. When you think about what we do today as QuestBank, we are primarily an alternative lender. We are working on expanding our product suite as we speak right now. But I think the biggest thing for brokers is just staying with their clients for longer.

[02:29] I think over the last couple years, people have reached a level of uncertainty that we haven't had in quite some time. Being in the alternative lending space gives us the opportunity to have a lot of really individual conversations with folks about their needs, the services and products that they require in order to find homes and stay in their homes comfortably. That's what we're trying to achieve through our entire product suite actually.

[02:51] Fergal McAlinden: And that growth in lending, we've seen it so much in recent years. It used to be kind of an optional last resort. That's increasingly not the case anymore. It's got to be a big opportunity for you there.

[03:03] Bekim Merdita: Yeah. Alternative lending just continues to grow. I think the reason why is simple. If you look at the stress test and how tight that can be on some borrowers, especially in modern times as values rose and incomes haven't kept up with inflation, it's just made it harder for a lot of people to qualify for traditional mortgages.

[03:20] And if you look at the terms and the rates available in alternative lending today, they're not the alternative lending products that people probably think about if they don't understand this industry. They're competitive rates, competitive terms, and they're prime clients for the most part. When you're looking at the profiles, these are good clients who pay their mortgages on time and ultimately just want to be in homes.

[03:42] Fergal McAlinden: It's hard to believe, but we're nearing the end of 2026. What about when you look ahead to next year? Obviously it's going to be a big one for you guys. Any trends you're keeping an eye on? Any thoughts on how the market's likely to play out next year?

[03:53] Bekim Merdita: As we look at next year and our current state right now, we're doing a lot of development on our side. If you're not working with AI today in the lending space, I think you're missing a massive opportunity. That's where our focus is right now.

[04:08] It's a combination of humans and technology. It's really about combining humans and technology for a more efficient lending organization. AI has just brought us into a new stratosphere in terms of what is possible. A lot of what used to be hard code is still hard code today. It's just that AI can do it so much faster. The human element is still the conversation, the understanding, and the empathy. We're building with those two things in mind.

[04:41] Fergal McAlinden: Is that still a learning curve? It must be interesting for you, having built startups before and worked in that space, and now we have the game changer of AI. It's got to be interesting to strike that balance between being human and AI.

[04:54] Bekim Merdita: I'll tell you this, my mind is blown every single week about what is possible with AI.

[04:58] Fergal McAlinden: Same here.

[04:59] Bekim Merdita: Everything that I once cooked up, I'm one of those mortgage nerds who will lay in bed at night and think about if we could just fix this and if we could just do that, and I don't have enough resources or time to build this or build that. What we are able to build now, even myself as a non-technical startup co-founder type individual, all my dreams about what can be built suddenly feel within reach.

[05:23] The question is not now can I build it, it's what do I build first and how fast can I go and is it going to make the impact that it has in my mind.

[05:31] Fergal McAlinden: Any thoughts for agents or brokers who are maybe a little bit nervous or skeptical about taking that first step with AI? I've been skeptical about it myself in the past, but it's increasingly becoming a part of everyone's lives. What should be the first step for them whenever they're adopting AI or looking to use it a little bit more?

[05:47] Bekim Merdita: When I think about AI and technology in the lending process and the broker process, there are a lot of ways in which one could implement it. I think the holy grail is ultimately getting into your workflows and having it act as basically an assistant to you or maybe a scary version, which is the duplication of who you are and what you do.

[06:07] I'm going to remove all of the work off my plate that I don't want to do. I think the early days were the LLM, the conversational structure. I'm going to ask it questions, it's going to give me answers. That in itself allowed me to move faster. It was like a better version of Google.

[06:23] But I think you ultimately want to skate where the puck is going. If you want to be on the forefront of the technology, you need to be asking yourself the question, how can I actually get this working in my workflows?

[06:35] You start to look at systems now that will actually jump into your workflow and start doing work on your behalf. And to your point, Fergal, it's about trust. If I'm an agent, if I'm a broker today, at some point I need to cross that threshold from being a skeptic to being a trusting individual who's going to use this, because if you don't, others will.

[06:52] Fergal McAlinden: Very well said. Last question for you, Bekim, before I let you go. The event today, have you been meeting your target audience? And what do you think the value of these types of events is for the industry?

[07:02] Bekim Merdita: I've seen so many familiar faces, which is amazing. And I've also seen so many new faces, and to me that's a really exciting part. Sometimes at industry events, you start to see all the same folks. What's really cool about this one especially is that I'm seeing so many people that I've never met before.

[07:19] I'm seeing people that are new to this industry, which is really exciting in a time where people are asking a lot of questions about what's my place as an individual in a space that is continually getting technology injected into it.

[07:30] This event, I think, brings together a lot of different folks from technology and traditional brick-and-mortar organizations, puts them in the same room, and gets discussions started. We start talking about the places in which we're different, we talk about the places in which we're the same, and we realize that we're all not so different after all.

[07:46] Fergal McAlinden: 100%. Very well said. All right. Great to catch up, my friend. Great to see you. Good luck on stage later on and all the best with the new role.

[07:52] Bekim Merdita: Yes. Thank you very much.

items.title: Housing costs affect wellbeing of 66% of Canadians, survey finds
items.description: Three in four mortgage holders report financial strain as retirement and debt plans are deferred
items.content: <p>Three in four mortgage holders report financial strain as retirement and debt plans are deferred</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312205380015366.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Three in four mortgage holders report financial strain as retirement and debt plans are deferred
items.body:
Housing costs are reshaping the lives of Canadians in ways that go well beyond the monthly mortgage statement — curtailing social connections, delaying retirement, and generating anxiety that now touches two in three Canadians nationwide.

A poll of 2,000 Canadian adults, commissioned by Peoples Group, a regulated Canadian financial services company, and Partners for Affordable Housing, a national nonprofit, found that 66% of Canadians say housing costs are affecting their wellbeing.

Among renters and homeowners with a mortgage, that figure climbs to 76%.

The survey was conducted online by Burson using Leger's panel between October 13 and October 27.

Some 24% of respondents experience a great deal or extreme stress from their housing situation, and fewer than half (48%) are confident they can manage those costs over the next 12 months.

The findings will resonate with brokers managing a client base under growing strain.

Dustan Woodhouse of Be The Better Broker, speaking to Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier in 2026 about the challenges facing first-time homebuyers in Canada's 2026 housing market, described a profession increasingly forced to deliver unwelcome answers.

"In the GTA and the GVA, that's become very compromised. It's very, very difficult. You're saying no to many people who come through the door now, even with prices falling as they have," he said.

Meanwhile, the number of Canadian bank mortgages at least 90 days past due reached 14,061 in May, the highest count in more than a decade, with the national arrears rate having more than doubled from a record low of 0.14% in 2022 to 0.29%, according to the Canadian Bankers Association.

Federal data points in the same direction. The 2024 Canadian Housing Survey, a collaboration between Statistics Canada and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC), found that 26.1% of mortgaged homeowners were living in housing they could not afford in 2024, up from 23.6% in 2022. 

When housing costs crowd out everything else

The survey maps what Canadians are sacrificing. Some 31% say they are seeing friends and family less often. Some 20% have reduced heating and cooling to manage costs.

Over the past year, 21% delayed paying down debt and 12% postponed retirement plans. That's consistent with federal data showing the financial squeeze on mortgaged homeowners across Canada released in September.

"Housing affordability is no longer just a housing issue; it's an economic one," said Aaron Cameron, SVP, Commercial Lending at Peoples Group in Canada.

"When housing costs take up a growing share of household income, Canadians have less capacity to save, invest and build long-term financial security."

New Ratehub .ca data shows home affordability declined across all 13 major Canadian housing markets in October as rising mortgage rates increased income requirements for buyers. https://t.co/2l9ocHRMfL — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

Building more is not enough

More than 27% of Canadians now spend over 30% of their household income on housing, the threshold Statistics Canada uses to define housing as unaffordable. 

"Addressing affordability requires action on multiple fronts," said Michel Cubric, SVP Deposits and Lending (Residential) at Peoples Group in Canada.

"The rules that govern residential development, including approval timelines, development charges, zoning and compliance costs, can have a significant impact on what Canadians ultimately pay for housing. Lasting affordability depends on building more homes and on a regulatory environment that makes them viable to deliver."

Were affordability not a constraint, 41% of Canadians say they would save or invest more, 19% would move toward homeownership, and 10% would pursue further education.

Partners for Affordable Housing launched its Address the Crisis campaign during National Housing Week, running November 22 to 28, calling on government, business, and community organisations to act collectively on housing supply.

items.description: Energy costs are still building in the system — Macklem says consumer pass-through is coming
items.content: <p>Energy costs are still building in the system — Macklem says consumer pass-through is coming</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639312186622596341.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Energy costs are still building in the system — Macklem says consumer pass-through is coming
items.body:
Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem on Tuesday warned that accumulated energy cost pressures have yet to fully reach consumers, sending market odds of a December rate hike to approximately 79%.

Speaking at the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on November 24, Macklem said recent crude oil price declines may bring year-end inflation slightly below the Bank's October projection of approximately 3.5%, but that the underlying cost build-up since the spring remains intact.

The speech coincided with the five-year renewal of Canada's monetary policy framework, reaffirming the 2% consumer price index (CPI) target within a 1% to 3% control range.

"So far, businesses have largely absorbed the higher production and transport costs," Macklem said in his prepared remarks.

"But historical lags and our own business surveys suggest more pass-through to consumer prices in the year ahead. This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence."

He also offered a candid assessment of the Bank's pandemic-era response. "We were too slow to recognize the persistence of inflationary pressures and how broadly they were spreading through the economy," Macklem acknowledged.

That lesson, he argued, underpinned the Bank's October rate hike. "The combination of increased inflation persistence and modestly better economic performance supported our decision in October to raise the policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5%."

Second-round effects to shape 2027 price outlook

Headline inflation held at 3.1% in October, unchanged from September, according to Statistics Canada, with high energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict the primary driver.

Macklem described a structurally more volatile world in which wars, trade conflict and extreme weather simultaneously push prices higher and slow economic output — a tension he said monetary policy cannot resolve without trade-offs.

"Inflation is likely to be pushed off course more frequently and for longer," he said.

Avery Shenfeld, chief economist at CIBC Capital Markets in Toronto, moved his December call forward.

"The Bank of Canada's speech seemed to downplay some of the disinflationary momentum seen of late, which points to a hike in December rather than our prior forecast, which leaned towards a January move," he wrote in a research note to clients on Tuesday, adding that the bank moved its forecast for the next hike to December from January.

December decision moves into focus for brokers

The Bank's final 2026 rate decision falls on December 9. The governing council will weigh third-quarter GDP figures due November 30 and the November Labour Force Survey on December 4 before deciding. 

Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker with LowestRates.ca in Toronto, said the cycle argument has hardened.

"If there is a hike, I do think it's going to be a cycle," she told Canadian Mortgage Professional following October's rate decision.

Macklem was clear on the Bank's mandate. "Monetary policy can't lower global energy prices," he said.

"But it can limit how much they spill over. Our goal is to avoid a situation where Canadians face rising prices for a wide range of goods and services."

The governor is set to step down when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027.

items._ogDesc: Ottawa is borrowing at a crisis pace without a crisis—pushing federal bond debt to $1.33 trillion and keeping Canadian fixed mortgage rates stubbornly high.
items.body:
Canada may not be in crisis, but federal borrowing suggests it’s in the middle of a pandemic-like event. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows a historic surge in Government of Canada (GoC) direct bonds in October. The single-month gain was the third-largest since COVID, and part of a much bigger wave of crisis-like borrowing not seen outside of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the pandemic. This doesn’t just limit the country’s options to respond to the next crisis—it all but eliminates the possibility of fixed-rate mortgage relief.

Government of Canada Direct Bonds Just Hit $1.33 Trillion

Total balance of outstanding federal bond issuance.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Total direct bonds surged 1.7% (+$22.8B) to $1.33 trillion in October, up 9.8% (+$118.9B) from last year. After a tame September (+$280M), net issuance made the third-largest monthly jump in dollar terms outside of the 2020-2021 pandemic. It trails only April 2023 and July 2025.

The climb is part of a broader trend of persistently elevated growth. Ottawa’s borrowing has logged 26 straight months of annual growth above 6% after the October gain. Over the past three years, the total has increased a mind-boggling 29.2% (+$301.7B). That’s right. Nearly 1 in 4 dollars of federal bond debt was added within three years, outside of the pandemic.

Canada’s Crisis-Like Borrowing Without A Crisis

Canadian policymakers are borrowing at a crisis pace without a crisis. Over the past 12 months, nominal dollar growth was 40.2% larger than the peak 12-month surge during the GFC. Outside of the GFC (2009-2012) and COVID (2020-2022), the balance hasn’t run this close to 10% annual growth since 1997. That was the tail end of Canada’s 1990s fiscal crunch, just as the last major real estate downturn was bottoming out.

The scale of borrowing won’t be easy to shake off. Since February 2020, the net bond balance has climbed 114.8%, more than doubling from pre-pandemic levels. Following a brief dip in 2023, growth came back with a vengeance—averaging 9.4% y/y over the past 24 months. That’s well above the 2010-2019 average of 6.6% on a much larger base. This has created a structural problem.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer has warned that interest payments will consume almost 1 in 7 dollars of revenue by 2030-31. More borrowing has driven debt-servicing costs to grow 29.5% faster than revenue, according to the agency. That would require nearly impossible revenue growth to catch up.

Ottawa’s Bond Supply Is Bad News For Mortgage Rate Relief

Heavy bond supply is set to put a drag on mortgage borrowing. Unlike variable mortgages that track the Bank of Canada’s overnight policy rate, fixed-rate loans are based on GoC bond yields (primarily the 5-year). The medium- and long-term impact of the bond balance may be abstract and debatable, but the short-term impact is crystal clear. It will limit any downside for mortgage rates, helping to build a floor.

For context, the GoC 5-year bond yield sat at 3.4% this morning, 74 basis points higher than last year. Those hoping for good news ahead of their mortgage renewal may not be so lucky, with BMO telling investors that rate relief is done for this phase of the cycle.

items.title: Mortgage delinquency rate up 31% in Q3, driven by Ontario and B.C.: Equifax report
items.description: TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
items._ogDesc: TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
items.body:
TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.

Equifax Canada's third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013.

That's up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.

"That's the highest we've seen, particularly for Ontario. And it's still going up," said Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada's vice-president of advanced analytics, said in an interview.

"That's the biggest concern for us."

The Equifax data echoes the findings of a recent a TD report, which showed Ontario's mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels to approach their 2008 financial crisis peak.

"This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs," wrote TD economist Maria Solovieva in the report published last week.

Growing pressure on households comes as the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month for the first time in more than three years, amid concerns that higher energy prices could spill into broader inflation.

The move prompted the big banks to raise their prime rates, which is used to set interest rates on a range of loans including variable-rate mortgages.

Equifax estimates about 1.4 million Canadians have a variable-rate mortgage out of a total 9.1 million homeowners. Another 1.3 million consumers also have a home equity line of credit, or HELOC, balance of more than $50,000.

Every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages, the company estimates.

Oakes suspects mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.

"If interest rates stay relatively flat from this point on, I'd expect to see it ease off in the middle of next year," she said.

But if more hikes come in, "it's just going to put additional pressure."

The central bank is expected to make its last rate decision of the year on Dec. 9.

Financial market odds for a quarter-point rate hike was 63 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

Oakes said first-time homebuyers and younger Canadians may bear the brunt of rising rates because they tend to carry a higher-balance mortgage.

Still, she said mortgage delinquencies overall are less than one per cent.

"It's quite small, you know, from that standpoint, but of course it knocks on to other types of credit, like credit cards, auto loans," Oakes said.

"That's where those individuals miss the payments first rather than on the mortgage itself."

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said Tuesday that he doesn't see rising mortgage delinquencies as a threat to the economy.

"Obviously for some people, this is very tough," he said in Toronto at an unrelated press conference. "But for the economy as a whole, it's not a huge headwind."Credit card balances reached $136.2 billion in the third quarter, up 4.82 per cent from a year earlier, the Equifax data showed.

Overall, total Canadian consumer debt was $2.74 trillion in the third quarter, up 4.68 per cent from a year ago.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

items.body:
Black Friday business was brisk and busy at the Halifax Shopping Centre, with discounts that shoppers said are too good to pass up.

“You get here and then you end up buying a little bit more than you expected,” said shopper Gilles Poirier, who also offered some advice for anyone who gets overwhelmed by busy shopping malls. “Usually, I come to the mall to get two or three things and then I grab those items and I quickly leave.”

Pop-up store manager Debbie Bowen said many Black Friday sales started earlier than in previous years, as far back as the first week in November.

“It has probably been three or four weeks in the mall with everyone posting their Black Friday sales,” Bowen said. “Saturday was crazy-busy in here.”

Annette Fralic drove more than 100 kilometres to shop Monday morning. Fralic said she usually shops with an open mind.

“And because of that I have most of my shopping done,” said Fralic, adding that when she spots a good deal, she often makes a quick purchase and loads up with Christmas presents.

“I told my daughter, I didn’t have a shopping list, yet here I am,” Fralic said, holding up several full shopping bags.

Some items at stores are already 60 per cent off, and a hot sauce vendor is offering a sizzling discount on dozens of flavours.

Retail analyst Bruce Winder said red-hot Black Friday deals will spark a 30 per cent increase in retail sales this week across the country. Combined with Cyber Monday, the retail industry in Canada could generate more than $10 billion in sales.

“We are seeing a lot of action on wireless noise-cancelling headphones,” Winder said. “Technology is always big at this time of the year. Video games like Grand Theft Auto VI are really big and so are toys, beauty products, floor-care products and winter apparel.”

“The average Black Friday shopper in Canada spends $300 or $400,” Winder said. “This week is really important for retailers to make money, which helps set the tone for their businesses for the rest of December.”

The Better Business Bureau (BBB) BBB.org has warned customers to use caution when shopping for Black Friday deals. Consumers should watch for fake websites and ads, buy only from trustworthy sellers on secure websites, check verified business reviews and make sure purchased items come with reliable return policies and warranties.

items.title: New Vancouver Council Approves Motion To Pursue Vacancy Control
items.description:
Vancouver has a new council. The make-up is very different from that of the previous council, and they wasted no time in their first meeting approving a suite of motions, reminding the city that they aren’t the same group as before.

Council is now led by the Green Party’s Pete Fry alongside four of his partymates, four members of the Coalition of Progressive Electors (COPE), one member of OneCity, and one member of ABC Vancouver.

The make-up of council now has a heavy progressive and left-of-centre lean, a stark contrast to the previous right-of-centre council where ABC had a supermajority.

Council was sworn in on November 2, and held their first regular council meeting on Tuesday, November 17, but the real action took place at the following day’s Standing Committee on City Finance and Services meeting, where a suite of motions introduced by various councillors were on the agenda.

The Universal Tenant Rights By-law

As it relates to housing, the most notable item was a motion introduced by COPE’s Sean Orr, who was elected in the 2025 by-election before being re-elected last month. The motion, titled “Enacting The Universal Tenant Rights By-law and Criminalizing Predatory Practices,” directed city staff to pursue a standalone tenant protection bylaw that would include:

1. Universal vacancy control;

2. Right of Return, including a “like for like” rule for replacement units;

3. 100% developer-funded bridge housing;

4. A “Fix the City” proactive inspection and repair mandate;

5. Democratic tenant oversight board: An elected (or randomly selected) body, with the power to oversee TRPP compliance;

6. Legal recognition of tenant unions;

7. “Fit and Proper” test for landlords, under section 272 of the Vancouver Charter, where predatory landlords lose the right to operate in the City; and

8. A public tenancy buyout registry, to provide transparency around landlord “cash for keys” offers.

Some of the asks already exists in one form or another, such as the Right of Return and developer funding of bridge housing, and others would not appear to have a huge impact on developers, but universal vacancy control is one that has drawn a strong reaction from the development industry.

Under current legislation in British Columbia, rents are only allowed to increase by a permitted amount each year, but landlords can raise the rent for a unit as much as they want in between tenancies. Vacancy control would prevent this.

Housing advocates argue that this practice results in landlords having an incentive to evict tenants, so they can then raise the rent for the unit, while the development industry argues that introducing vacancy control would significantly impact the economics of developing rental buildings and result in less new construction.

Construction lawyer Tim M. Sportschuetz said in a LinkedIn post that vacancy control “risks becoming the death knell for new rental construction and small-scale private landlords in Vancouver” and “introduces long-term uncertainty into rental revenues, making financing more difficult and discouraging the very construction Vancouver desperately needs.”

On the other side of the argument, the Vancouver Tenants Union (VTU) said it was “pleased that COPE Councillors are treating the issues facing tenants as a priority in their first days on Council,” noting that Orr’s motion includes “items that the VTU has advocated for over many years, such as vacancy control, strengthening bylaw enforcement against landlords, and enabling the city to remove business licenses from landlords who are non-compliant.”

The motion was passed unanimously and City staff are now expected to present the proposed by-law in Q1 2027, although it’s currently unclear whether the City would actually have the authority to enact vacancy control, as tenancies are governed by the provincial Residential Tenancy Act.

Moisture Monitoring

The next motion discussed was also pertaining to rental housing. Entitled “Moisture Monitoring and Prevention Standards in Residential Rental Housing,” the motion was introduced by Mayor Pete Fry and builds off of the “Enhanced Tools for Standards of Property Maintenance” motion he introduced in April 2025 that was approved.

The previous motion directed staff to explore amendments to the Standards of Maintenance By-law pertaining to mould, water damage, and indoor air quality, and the new motion adds moisture management to the list while also asking staff to report back on opportunities to strengthen the by-law.

Potential options include establishing thresholds for excessive moisture content, moisture content testing, building envelope assessments, and options to potentially require landlords to investigate and remediate the source of excessive moisture.

This motion was also approved.

Repealing The Supportive Housing Ban

When then-Mayor Ken Sim introduced a motion calling for a temporary pause on net new supportive housing investments in February 2025, it became a lightning rod, and supportive housing became one of the biggest election issues.

The Green Party, COPE, and OneCity all ran on platforms that included ending/repealing that temporary ban, and Orr introduced a motion titled “Housing With Supports: Improving Public Safety by Tackling Root Causes” to follow through on that, asking City staff to report back on the potential impacts of repealing the temporary ban.

The motion was again approved, after Council also reversed the previous council’s 2023 decision to dissolve the Vancouver Park Board. (Orr also introduced “The People’s Audit,” a motion calling for a report on staffing changes that were made as a result of ABC’s decision for a 0% property tax increase for 2026.)

Tax Avoidance for Unbuilt Housing Sites

The last big housing-related motion considered was entitled “Strengthening Safeguards Against Tax Avoidance for Unbuilt Housing Sites.” It was introduced by OneCity’s Lucy Maloney, who was elected in the 2025 by-election and was re-elected last month, and targets a practice that has been discussed on-and-off over the years: community gardens.

Many developers have numerous land holdings and wait for the right time to proceed with a project. In addition to just waiting, however, some developers convert the vacant land into a community garden in order to change the tax classification of the property and reduce their property tax obligations. The oft-cited example (and example Maloney pointed to in her motion) is Holborn Group with their Little Mountain project, although there are many other examples.

Maloney’s motion asks Council to “establish defining safeguards against tax avoidance for unbuilt housing sites as a priority for this term in order to ensure continued housing development” and also asks staff to explore potential ways to amend the permitting process for community gardens and to “compensate for the impact on other taxpayers.”

As with the other motions, this one was approved.

items._ogDesc: Canadian household debt hit $3.3T in September as mortgage growth fell to a 25-year low, while consumer credit ran hot on rising distress borrowing.
items.body:
Canadian household debt is slowing in growth, but it doesn’t appear to be voluntary deleveraging. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows household credit climbed in September, though mortgages are contributing less. The segment grew at one of the slowest paces in a quarter-century, even as consumer credit took off alongside rising distress borrowing.

Canadian Household Debt Hits $3.3 Trillion Even As Growth Slows

Annual growth of Canadian household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadian household debt climbed 0.3% (+$9.4 billion) to hit $3.3 trillion in September, 3.7% (+$119.3 billion) higher than last year. It’s a sharp deceleration from the 4.6% annual growth reported this time a year ago, suggesting household borrowing is slowing. Even at a slower pace, adding over $119 billion in a single year is hardly deleveraging. Households are just lightly tapping the brakes.

Canadian Mortgage Credit Growth Slows To Lowest Pace In 25 Years

Annual growth of Canadian mortgage credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Mortgage growth appears to be the big drag here. Outstanding mortgage credit rose 0.2% (+$4.9 billion) to $2.47 trillion in September, 3.5% (+$82.6 billion) from last year. This is the slowest annual growth for mortgage credit since mid-2001. In an economy as housing-dependent as Canada’s, a quarter-century low in mortgage expansion signals that buyers are either tapped out or stuck on the sidelines.

Distress Borrowing Keeps Consumer Credit Running Hot At $847 Billion

Annual growth of Canadian non-mortgage household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

One area of credit growth that continues to run hot is consumer credit. Households grew non-mortgage debt by 0.5% (+$4.5 billion) to $847.0 billion in September, up 4.5% (+$36.7 billion). While slower than August, the annual growth of this segment has been higher than usual over the past few years, sustaining levels the country hasn’t seen since mid-2010. Healthy credit growth can sometimes be a sign of strong consumers, but this isn’t one of those times.

Credit reporting bureaus are increasingly attributing growth to distress borrowing. Firms like TransUnion have noted that more borrowers are carrying higher balances as they use credit to make ends meet. Mortgage borrowers aren’t much better, with the bureau also explaining that a rising share of mortgage debt is due to accumulating balances, not originations.

Slowing headline growth may look like restraint on the surface, but it’s a more ominous sign. There are few signs of relief ahead, as the market expects higher borrowing costs.

items.title: Fengate, Capital Developments Buy TAS Leslieville Site Out Of Receivership For $16M
items.description:
Another development site formerly owned by Toronto-based developer TAS has been sold under receivership, according to filings in Ontario Superior Court and transaction details obtained by STOREYS.

The site is 880 Eastern Avenue and 80 Knox Avenue in the Leslieville neighbourhood of Toronto, a few blocks west of Ashbridges Bay and Woodbine Park.

TAS acquired 80 Knox Avenue in 2020 with a first-ranking mortgage in the principal amount of $10.3 million that was provided by Canadian Mortgage Servicing Corporation (CMSC) — a subsidiary of Canadian Mortgage Capital Corporation (CMCC) — and acquired 880 Eastern Avenue via a $4.32 million vendor take-back mortgage provided by Michael & Michael Auto Body Ltd.

In September 2022, the CMSC loan was then amended to facilitate the acquisition of 874 and 876 Eastern Avenue for $2.5 million “to have additional adjacent lands available for the benefit of the intended development,” according to court documents.

For the site, TAS was planning a 12-storey building with 184 rental units and 10,000 sq. ft of commercial space on the ground floor — the numbers have been updated multiple times — and the project was once set to become Toronto’s first net-zero mid-rise residential building.

The properties were beneficially owned by TAS through 880EA Corp. and 874EA Corp. while TAS LP 3 served as the guarantor of the CMSC loan.

The Insolvency

According to CMSC, the loan matured in February 2025, TAS stopped making interest payments in July 2025, and also failed to make property tax payments. It also took out another mortgage from Toronto-based private equity real estate investment firm KingSett Capital in March 2025 without obtaining consent from CMSC. (KingSett Capital was also a lender to TAS on their Labatt Village project.)

CMSC issued a formal demand for payment in August 2025 and said it was owed $10,734,679.39 as of August 13, 2025, with interest continuing to accrue. After the borrowers could not repay the debt, CMSC initiated the receivership proceeding.

In its application, CMSC noted there was a “protracted sale effort” pertaining to the properties that began around May 2024 and ran for about a year. The property was listed by Dan Rogers, Jeff Lever, Reilly Hayhurst, and Mike Murray of Cushman & Wakefield as a “partnership or sale opportunity,” according to the sales brochure.

CMSC said the previous sale attempt was unsuccessful and that they wanted to have the project placed under receivership so it can be sold free and clear of all claims.

“I believe that an immediate sale will maximize the value of the Secured Properties for the benefit of all stakeholders,” said CMSC’s Managing Director in a September 2025 affidavit. “Moreover, the situation is an ongoing risk whereby CMSC’s security position may erode.”

The Sale Process

The project approved for 880 Eastern Avenue and 80 Knox Avenue. (SvN Architects, TAS)

The development site was placed under receivership on September 17, 2025, and the court-ordered sales process commenced shortly afterwards. Although the court-appointed Receiver opened up the process to other brokers, they ultimately re-engaged Cushman & Wakefield due to the work they had already done.

The Receiver said there was “significant market interest,” with 31 parties signing confidentiality agreements and 8 parties submitting bids by the December 9 deadline. However, the Receiver and Cushman were “dissatisfied with all offers received” and decided to open a new sales process, this time including the possibility of a vendor take-back (VTB) mortgage funding a portion of the purchase price.

Although Toronto-based developer Capital Developments did not submit an offer in the initial sale process, it remained interested and eventually submitted an offer in the second round, which was accepted by the Receiver on February 9. The sale agreement was amended in March, April, and July before it was finalized and then approved by the Ontario Superior Court on September 23.

“In conjunction with the closing, the Receiver proposes to assign the VTB to CMSC and M&M in its entirety,” said the Receiver in a report. “In the case of M&M, the Receiver proposes to assign the portion of the VTB up to the value of its debt, inclusive of interest as at the date of closing.”

“While an ideal scenario would have resulted in a cash only purchase price for the Real Property, the Receiver and Cushman & Wakefield are of the view that the current environment required structured finance by way of the VTB to maximize the purchase price and provide the highest recovery to affected stakeholders,” the Receiver added.

Notably, 874 and 876 Eastern Avenue were left out of the sale, and the Receiver said there were no bids at any point for the two properties.

The Project

The purchase agreement was originally signed by CD Capital Developments (Acquisitions) Limited in February, but the final agreement was instead signed on July 31 by 880 Eastern Limited Partnership.

The final sale price was redacted from court documents, but according to an Altus Group transaction report obtained by STOREYS, 880 Eastern Avenue and 80 Knox Avenue transacted on October 15 for $16,000,000, with $10,250,000 funded in cash and $5,750,000 funded by the vendor take-back mortgage.

On October 27, Fengate Asset Management then announced that it had established a joint venture with Capital Developments, with Fengate managing the investment on behalf of the LiUNA Pension Fund of Central and Eastern Canada and Capital Developments making the acquisition through Address, its rental platform.

“Toronto’s population continues to grow, and the supply of high-quality rental housing has not kept pace,” said Jaime McKenna, President, Fengate Real Estate. “We are thrilled to be partnering with Address, a team that shares our commitment to delivering more housing for our city. Together, we are unlocking new rental supply in Leslieville and creating a connected community where people can live and work, with convenient access to transit, the waterfront and everyday amenities.”

The partners said they plan to develop more than 250 rental units, including affordable rental units, suggesting the project may look different than what was previously approved. Construction is expected to begin in late-2027.

A recent report from REMAX Canada notes the luxury residential real estate market across Canada demonstrated a regional divide through the first nine months of 2026.

Smaller markets led sales growth, while major metropolitan centres saw buyer hesitation, with the overall luxury market in Greater Vancouver (-17 per cent) and the Greater Toronto Area (-9.4 per cent) recording contractions.
